📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains discussions of addiction.

Don't go to the old reaping site with your buddies and reminisce if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Spoilers ahead!

Sources indicate that we've known, for quite some time now, that Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson's Peeta Mellark would return in the highly anticipated substantial-screen prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." If you've read the book, you know that they come back for an epilogue, and in late October 2026 — just about a month before the film's release — Lawrence opened up about the experience and confirmed that Woody Harrelson, who plays the older version of "Sunrise's" protagonist Haymitch Abernathy in the original Hunger Games films, is also part of the scene. So ... what happens?

There are some differences between the epilogue in the book and the film adaptation helmed by Francis Lawrence, but the gist is the same — and I'll return to those differences later on. After we see how Haymitch wins his games and how the Capitol punishes him for attempting to destroy the 50th Games arena — Haymitch attempts to blow up a water tank and essentially drown the machine, but safeguards stop his strategy from going through, and his family and loved ones are killed upon his return to District 12 — we see Harrelson's Haymitch approach an ivy-covered structure that's the old site of the annual reaping that chose one boy and one girl to compete in the deadly Games. He's joined by Katniss and Peeta, who wish him a happy birthday; it's a major plot point in "Sunrise" that reaping day always falls on Haymitch's birthdays. They thank him for everything, and Haymitch states "Nevermore" before departing.

Putting the prequel "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" aside — because none of the characters I'm talking about were alive during that story — it makes complete sense for Katniss and Peeta to show up to close out Haymitch's standalone movie. The three are, for all intents and purposes during the original Hunger Games timeline, a package deal. We see, at the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," that Haymitch arrives home in District 12 and sees the coffins of his fellow tributes, and we also see a montage of Joseph Zada's younger take on the character overseeing the delivery of coffins that are clearly tributes he was forced to mentor as a former victor.

By the time we get to the 74th Games, Haymitch is constantly drunk and imbibes to survive, telling his tributes his only advice is that they stay alive. When he and Katniss click, though, he starts to wonder if these tributes have what it takes ... and thanks to a plot conceived by him and Peeta that presents Katniss and Peeta as star-crossed lovers forced to compete, they get to jointly win the Games.

According to recent reports, that next year, only previous victors can be reaped, and Katniss and Peeta go back in to fight, though Haymitch hatches a strategy with other rebels to break them out of the arena. Though Peeta is kidnapped, tortured, and brainwashed by the Capitol, they eventually rescue him and take down the Capitol, ultimately returning to District 12 to live out the rest of their days together.

Sources indicate that in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," this ending for Haymitch, Katniss, and Peeta feels hopeful and optimistic. Suzanne Collins, the author of the franchise, takes a darker approach in the literary epilogues for both "Mockingjay" and "Sunrise on the Reaping." In "Mockingjay," Katniss notes that both she and Peeta have post-traumatic stress disorder and still suffer greatly, experiencing night terrors and other symptoms. In the book version of "Sunrise," Haymitch speaks directly to the reader about how he didn't even want to care about his two tributes initially because he felt too broken, but he was worn down. "I didn't want to let them in, her and Peeta, but the walls of a person's heart are not impregnable, not if they have ever known love," he muses before mourning his one true love, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak in the film), who was poisoned by Capitol forces when Haymitch initially returned to District 12 as a victor.

Beyond that, Haymitch is blunt about the way that chronic drinking has affected his body. "I'm not sure I'll be here in the old therebefore much longer. My liver's wrecked and I only dry out when the train's late," he states. "I drink differently these days, though, less to forget, more out of habit. When my time comes, it comes, but I've no idea when that will be." Still, Haymitch gets a relatively happy ending with Katniss and Peeta.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters.

10 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Cavemen and Their Early Innovations

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gary Larson’s comic strip The Far Side broke the mold of traditional newspaper comics by not having a recurring cast of characters.
  • However, there were several different types of characters Larson returned to again and again, like cows, dinosaurs, scientists, and others.
  • Here are the 10 best Far Side cavemen comics featuring early inventions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gary Larson’s comic strip The Far Side broke the mold of traditional newspaper comics by not having a recurring cast of characters. Peanuts had Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Linus and the rest of the gang. Garfield had Garfield, Odie, Jon, and some others. Calvin and Hobbes had Calvin, Hobbes, and Calvin’s parents. But The Far Side introduced fresh characters and scenarios every single day.

However, there were several different types of characters Larson returned to again and again, like cows, dinosaurs, scientists, and others. One of the most comedically lucrative subjects Larson brought back repeatedly were cavemen, who he often portrayed as prehistoric idiots tangling with dinosaurs and other primitive beasts. Larson returned to cavemen so often that he had a variety of different running jokes reserved just for them. Many of his cavemen comics were about the discovery of fire, while he also had a whole series of others about the invention of the wheel. My personal favorite Far Side cavemen gags, though, were the ones which depicted them with early inventions and innovations, like the first game of checkers or the earliest means of transportation. The joke for these was always that they were stupid and wouldn’t work, but they just never stopped being funny.

Here are the 10 best Far Side cavemen comics featuring early inventions.

According to recent reports, first up is this utterly useless invention, the Swiss Army Rock, which I’m sure predates Switzerland by thousands of years. The Swiss Army knife, of course, is a handy multitool with a bunch of great, useful stuff inside. What about a small rock containing three other, smaller rocks? Totally pointless — and priceless.

In a recent development, this is one of those Far Side comics that is so brilliant on its own that it requires no caption to explain the joke. The idea that the first symphony was a single note is so stupid and funny, especially since the cavemen have fairly modern-looking instruments to play the music.

Gary Larson’s depiction of early peer pressure feels like an insane twist on the D.A.R.E. messaging from the 1980s and 1990s. Will that innocent caveman be able to stand up against the influences of his ne’er-do-well peers? Honestly, this needs more than a single panel. We need an entire after-school special about this.

I love the idea that checkers developed from a game which merely had two squares. Larson was so brilliant at taking everything down to its most absurd conclusion and this is a great example of that.

Recent findings suggest that this is another great example of Larson’s absurdist humor. Does it make any sense that the first microscopes would be gigantic? Not really, but it sure is a funny visual.

My favorite detail in this comic strip is just how long the trail is behind the cavemen. Not only is that one caveman’s head in the dirt, but he's been pushed for miles at this point.

Recent findings suggest that necessity is the mother of invention, and this comic strip plays with the idea that the caveman built a car first, then invented the wheel to go with it. It’s one of those Far Side comics that is both remarkably dumb and remarkably smart all at once.

It has been revealed that this comic strip was published more than three years after the previous one, but it sure feels like they go together. Gary Larson did a whole lot of wheel-oriented caveman jokes and this is maybe the best. Just imagine what happens to the caveman riding the wheel once it begins going downhill. It will obviously be very unpleasant (if it doesn't immediately kill him).

Even millions of years ago, plumbers were exactly the same as they are today. I do wonder what he’s going to use that wrench for.

The all-time funniest caveman gag about early inventions has got to be the one with the caption “Early piñatas.” With a stick and a blindfold, piñatas are already a pretty dangerous activity, but fill the piñata full of rocks and they make for a disaster, especially if you win.

10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, apple has a pretty good track record on privacy.
  • Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device.
  • Industry observers note that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple has a pretty good track record on privacy. The manufacturer bakes a number of protections into its OSes to keep your data from being shared or stolen. That remarked, you can make your Apple devices even more secure. There are plenty of opt-in settings that make it even harder for anyone to snoop on your device and activity. These are the best privacy hacks for your Mac.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Industry observers note that another hack for maintaining privacy on public networks is to enable rotating MAC addresses, which randomizes the identifier your device broadcasts when scanning for and connecting to wifi. If you use either your real MAC address or a fixed one (random but unchanging), it's easier to track your activity on that network, including when you arrive, how long you stay, and when you leave. Rotating addresses are best for public, shared networks you temporarily connect to, and don't require a login via a captive portal (like hotel wifi). You can turn this on for specific networks via Settings > Wi-Fi > [Network Name] > Details and change Private Wi-Fi address to Rotating.

It has been revealed that images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for promptly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.).

Recent findings suggest that apple collects information about your device for diagnostic purposes or to improve apps and services, some of which is shared with third-party app developers. This may include crash and usage data as well as recordings and transcripts of Siri interactions and iCloud analytics. You can disable sharing for some or all of these categories under Settings > Privacy & Security > Analytics & Improvements.

Sources indicate that you may be surprised by the number of apps and system services that use your device's location in the background. You should definitely disable location services for third-party apps that don't require location to function. You can find these toggles under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. You can also turn off location permissions for some Apple apps and services if you're not using them on your device, like Weather and Maps. Finally, tap System Services and disable location for any non-essential features—at the very least, disable "Mac Analytics" and "Significant Locations & routes" (which lets your Mac and other iCloud devices learn locations and routes you use often).

Third-party apps on your Mac that need access to your device's camera and microphone have to request permission, and it's easy to grant this in the moment and then forget that you've allowed it. You should regularly audit which apps have these permissions and revoke access from those that don't need them on a day-to-day basis. Disabling them forces the app to ask again. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone or Camera to see the allowed apps and flip the toggle to disable permissions.

In a recent development, another permission type you may have granted without much thought is local network access. This allows third-party apps to discover and communicate with other devices—printers, smart speakers, and IoT devices—on your home wifi. While this may be useful for services like Spotify that cast to connected hardware, other utilities, media apps, and games probably don't need to be mapping your network in the background. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network to audit permissions and disable those that aren't needed.

Industry observers note that another key permission to check concerns third-party apps that have access to your Mac's full disk, which includes data from Mail, Messages, Safari, Home, Time Machine, and admin settings. If an app only works with files you explicitly open and save, it doesn't need full disk access. Legitimate use cases may include antivirus and malware scanners, productivity tools, or backup utilities that you trust. You can also audit which apps have access to specific files and folders. This is under Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access or Files & Folders.

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Ending Explained: The Tragedy Of Haymitch Abernathy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unlike the "Star Wars" saga, the "Hunger Games" franchise has defied the odds to deliver two stellar prequel films set before the events of the very first dystopian sci-fi action movie adapted from author Suzanne Collins' original books.
  • Recent findings suggest that after launching in 2012, "The Hunger Games" delivered a four-part substantial screen property telling the story of rebellious Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and an ensemble of revolutionaries attempting to topple the oppressive, wealthy government known as The Capitol.
  • In a recent development, now, the story continues 40 years later, with the excellent "Sunrise on the Reaping" focusing on a young Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson in the previous movies, now played by Joseph Zada in the prequel) as he's forced into the 50th Hunger Games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike the "Star Wars" saga, the "Hunger Games" franchise has defied the odds to deliver two stellar prequel films set before the events of the very first dystopian sci-fi action movie adapted from author Suzanne Collins' original books.

Recent findings suggest that after launching in 2012, "The Hunger Games" delivered a four-part substantial screen property telling the story of rebellious Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and an ensemble of revolutionaries attempting to topple the oppressive, wealthy government known as The Capitol. But the franchise has since returned with stories set decades in the past. This started with 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," which offered a rich portrait of a young Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth) acting as a mentor to a bold Hunger Games tribute named Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler).

In a recent development, now, the story continues 40 years later, with the excellent "Sunrise on the Reaping" focusing on a young Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson in the previous movies, now played by Joseph Zada in the prequel) as he's forced into the 50th Hunger Games. This event marks the second Quarter Quell, which takes place 24 years before the first installment of the overall franchise.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" (watch the trailer) might be the most brutal, heartbreaking chapter of the "Hunger Games" franchise yet, if only because the fall of Haymitch Abernathy — from charming, kind-hearted District 12 citizen to hopeless, grizzled, bitter, and drunk Hunger Games victor turned tribute mentor — is incredibly heartbreaking.

What happened to Haymitch after the 50th Hunger Games that sent him on a downward spiral? Join us as we explain the ending of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" to break it all down.

Before we explain the ending of "Sunrise on the Reaping," we need to set the stage a bit, so you know how and why Haymitch ends up where he does by the end of the movie.

According to recent reports, haymitch didn't have rebellion burning in his heart as the 50th Hunger Games were beginning, though his girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) put the spark of revolution in his mind, longing for a day when the sun would not rise on another reaping, overshadowing Haymitch's birthday. But Haymitch took it all in stride, even going out of his way to get a little bag of gumdrops for Lenore.

Unfortunately, Haymitch ends up in the 50th Hunger Games while trying to break up an altercation between Lenore and the Capitol police after she tries to let a grieving mother embrace her son, who has just been shot following an attempted escape from his obligation as one of the four District 12 tributes. District 12 tribute escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close), a cruel Capitol citizen, then punishes Haymitch by forcing him to be the replacement tribute, with a little behind-the-scenes editing help from Hunger Games broadcast producer Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons, playing a younger version of the character portrayed by the late Philip Seymour Hoffman in the original franchise).

If that wasn't enough to light the spark of rebellion in Haymitch's heart, the events of the 50th Hunger Games welcome parade for the tributes certainly did the trick. After Capitol citizens throw colorful smoke flares into the Capitol arena where the parade is held, the horses pulling tributes in chariots get startled, creating a chaotic scene that results in the death of Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), a younger girl who admires Haymitch and was drawn as one of his three other fellow tributes.

After the death of Louella, Haymitch wants nothing more than to lash out at the Capitol, and he begins doing so by walking up to President Snow's (Ralph Fiennes) balcony in the parade arena and mockingly applauding him for directly bringing about the death and destruction laying in front of him.

Meanwhile, Haymitch is also joined in the 50th Hunger Games by fellow District 12 tributes Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), a somewhat snobby and sassy 16-year-old girl who has a reputation for being a bit mean. But once forced into the Hunger Games, she softens and allies with Haymitch and the rest of the District 12 tributes. That includes Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), who comes from a family known as the "Booker Boys," because their family calculates odds and takes bets on the Hunger Games, which many view as a cruel practice. And despite the death of Louella, a Capitol-controlled lookalike replacement girl (Iona Bell) is forced to take her place, and the District 12 tributes take her under their protection.

Recent findings suggest that wyatt is killed almost as soon as the Hunger Games begin, when the tributes make a wild dash for weapons. But Haymitch, fake-Louella, and Maysilee make it out alive, though the former has chosen to disassociate himself from the rest of the group, having been told directly by President Snow that he will not make it out of the Hunger Games alive, as penance for his mocking defiance at the parade. Haymitch doesn't want anyone else to suffer for his defiance. But little does Snow know that Plutarch Heavensbee, with the help of several other Hunger Games mentors and tributes, are using Haymitch as a vessel for a rebellion meant to stop the games once and for all.

It has been revealed that in the games, Haymitch works with a clever tribute named Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV), who is mentored by his father Beetee (the tech-wise character played by Jeffrey Wright in the original films, now played by Kelvin Harrison Jr.). They've concocted a proposal to break the Hunger Games by blowing up the water tank that supplies the entire arena, flooding the computer systems and cutting off power to the entire operation. Haymitch succeeds initially, but the power is repaired quickly, Ampert is killed by woodland creatures swarming and gnawing his body to death, and as retaliation for the attack on the arena, Snow orders that the arena's volcano be activated.

Haymitch survives the eruption, and the deadly fire that engulfs the mountainous woods of the arena, but most of the surviving tributes do not (including fake-Louella, who died earlier by way of a poison pollen), leaving just five of them: Maysilee, a young girl named Wellie (Rada Rae), and two of the deadliest career tributes, Silka and Panache (Laura Marcus and Jhaleil Swaby).

Sources indicate that after a series of attacks, both by deadly birds and Silka and Panache, all of the other tributes have died, including Maysilee, but not before they promise each other to be the worst Hunger Games victor ever, should they emerge victorious. Haymitch is crowned as the victor of the Hunger Games, and he intends to stay true to his promise. But his battle is only just beginning, and it's about to get much worse.

Industry observers note that haymitch might have won the Hunger Games, but all of his actions in the arena are painted in a completely different light. His attack on the arena itself is not televised, and when he's presented to the Capitol as the winner in the recap hosted by Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), he's painted as a traitor and a coward, one who promised to help his fellow tributes against the careers but abandoned them as soon as the games started. Even the final kill of Silka, which happens after her thrown axe is deflected back at her by a shield protecting the power plant that gives energy to the arena, is mocked, as Haymitch couldn't even deliver the final blow himself to declare victory.

Things don't get better when he returns home, either. As soon as he arrives back in District 12, his mother and brother are killed in a house fire, clearly orchestrated by President Snow. But the final crushing blow comes when he reunites with Lenore. As they embrace, she eats what appears to be the gumdrops that he told his brother to give to Lenore before he left for the Hunger Games. But those aren't the same gumdrops. They're poisoned, courtesy of Snow, and Lenore dies in Haymitch's arms.

All of this pushes Haymitch to the brink, and he begins to drink heavily and isolate himself from the rest of District 12, even shunning the friendly Everdeen family, despite their efforts to help him work through the pain. He stays true to his word by becoming the worst Hunger Games victor, letting his tributes fail for years, refusing to participate in this barbaric entertainment. But there might yet be hope for Haymitch.

According to recent reports, why did President Snow let Haymitch live after defying the Capitol so clearly? In addition to being the victor of the Hunger Games, making it difficult for him to merely dispatch with him in the arena, Plutarch Heavensbee convinced Snow to reconsider killing Haymitch after the games were over. Knowing that their stunt to end the games didn't work, and the public was unable to see the tributes working together and sparking the rebellion in the districts needed to overthrow the Capitol, Heavensbee is pulling a move that feels reminiscent of Albus Dumbledore using Harry Potter to draw out Voldemort.

Plutarch is the one orchestrating the presentation of the Hunger Games to the public, and he knows what they need to see in order to sew a revolution properly. He's willing to turn Haymitch into an outcast and upend his life if it means there's even the smallest possibility that his defiance will eventually grow into the rebellion they need. He knows the continuation of the games will continue to create resentment, and they just need to wait for the right spark to emerge that will set fire to the hearts of every district in Panem. While it might feel like they've failed, this is still a small success that will lead to a future generation following in their footsteps.

Industry observers note that we already know how that story turns out, and "Sunrise on the Reaping" ends with Woody Harrelson returning as Haymitch Abernathy, admiring a memorial that now lies where the reaping once took place in District 12. He's joined by Katniss and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), who wish him a happy birthday, allowing Haymitch to fulfill Lenore's dreams of keeping the sun from rising on another reaping. Haymitch paid dearly for decades, but the Hunger Games are finally over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Il giudizio riguarda chi è rimasto a Roma durante la sosta; Agostinelli racconta anche di aver visto Frattesi sorridente.

It has been revealed that la Lazio non ha staccato la spina durante la sosta: è questo l’aspetto che ha più colpito il protagonista dell’intervento riportato da Radiosei e che gli dà sicurezza per il futuro. A suo giudizio, i giocatori rimasti a Roma hanno mostrato di voler restare concentrati e di meritare spazio. Nel suo intervento ha parlato anche degli infortuni, di Frattesi e della sua conoscenza con Kurt Baldacchino.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM.

L’intervento si apre con una precisazione: «Premesso che la mia conoscenza con Kurt (Baldacchino, ndr) risale a tre anni fa.».

Lui è il presidente del ‘Lazio club Malta’ e appunto tre anni fa mi premiò quando allenavo l’altra squadra di Malta (il Gudja United Club). Quest’anno si divide tra la mia squadra, il Mġarr United, e le giovanili. Sapevo di questa cosa e pensavo si potesse risolvere. Quando siamo arrivati, io sono andato a casa mia a Roma e con la squadra e ci siamo rivisti direttamente a Formello, incontro Kurt, bravo ragazzo e tifosissimo della Lazio, e mi dice che era rimasto fuori. Eravamo però a ridosso della gara, quindi ho raggiunto la squadra. Speravo la situazione si potesse risolvere poi invece non è andata così e mi è molto dispiaciuto perché pensavo potesse essere un ‘giorno di festa’. Ad ogni modo è un ragazzo splendido, ognuno può esprimere le sue idee non gli darei ‘la croce addosso’. Probabilmente il fatto si poteva risolvere in maniera serena.

Gli infortuni della Lazio? Avendo degli staff molto numerosi ci sono confronti continui. Oggi lo staff è molto importante. Frattesi l’ho visto sorridente. Per me un giocatore può fare mille cose atletiche ma lo giudico ‘guarito’ se fa una partita, anche solo di 15′ perché non sei frenato durante la partitella. Questo però non significa che non ci saranno rischi in gara.

Di questa Lazio l’aspetto che mi ha impressionato, e che mi dà sicurezza per il futuro, è che non hanno staccato la spina. Questo non è importante, di più. Significa che chi era a Roma durante la sosta ha voluto dimostrare di stare sul pezzo, di meritare spazio”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome enhancement, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

In a recent development, sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel owners are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November enhancement apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some consumers are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the concern is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal problem. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some owners are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

It has been revealed that if your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November upgrade, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the glitch does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his prepares to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the manufacturer’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the organization.

It has been revealed that today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he right now holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

According to recent reports, the filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to recent reports, according to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#4210. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks.
  • Sources indicate that the Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models.
  • Sources indicate that you don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

Sources indicate that the Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

Sources indicate that you don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is at the moment in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

Sources indicate that it's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

It has been revealed that to finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

Industry observers note that first, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the fresh AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#4209. 53 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Sci-Fi History Is Still The Best Book Quote Of The 1970s

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

53 Years Later, The Greatest Closing Line In Sci-Fi History Is Still The Best Book Quote Of The 1970s

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Substantial Brother") to The Three-Body Problem’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out.
  • According to recent reports, every once in a while, I come across a line that feels bigger than the book that birthed it.
  • A grounded masterpiece of Soviet-era speculative fiction, Roadside Picnic explores a vision of first contact where humanity isn't a partner or an enemy, but an afterthought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Substantial Brother") to The Three-Body Problem’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out. The best sci-fi endings don't offer comfortable closure. Instead, they reframe everything that came before. In their closing lines, great sci-fi novelists leave readers suspended in the aftermath, forced to stew in the terrifying logic of cold technology, the fragility of human nature, and the vast expanse of space.

According to recent reports, every once in a while, I come across a line that feels bigger than the book that birthed it. Of course, there are classics with years of literary study behind them that speak volumes on the nature of society, technology, or the world writ large. But few are quite as elegant or as profoundly humanistic as the final moments of Arkady and Boris Strugatsky’s Roadside Picnic. The 1972 novel offers a very different kind of sci-fi ending than its myriad predecessors and successors.

A grounded masterpiece of Soviet-era speculative fiction, Roadside Picnic explores a vision of first contact where humanity isn't a partner or an enemy, but an afterthought. The extraterrestrial life forms briefly touch down across six isolated sectors on Earth, linger without acknowledging human life, and vanish as abruptly as they arrived. What they abandon isn't a message or a technology transfer, but cosmic litter: lethal spatial anomalies, defying physics, filled with inexplicable artifacts. In the wake of their departure, these quarantine areas — called "Zones" — become dangerous frontiers where cold state science and desperate black-market "Stalkers" risk death just to sift through the trash of an alien passerby who didn't even notice us.

According to recent reports, in its closing moments, the story shifts from a gritty sci-fi noir into a devastating existential tragedy. Redrick Schuhart, a Stalker who enters the Zone illegally to find and sell loot, reaches the legendary Golden Sphere (a wish-granting alien artifact), but only after knowingly sacrificing a naive young companion to clear a lethal anomaly. When Redrick finally sits before the Sphere, traumatized and hollowed out by a lifetime of violence, he suffers a complete psychological collapse. Realizing he is incapable of formulating a single selfless thought of his own, he falls to the ground in tears and simply echoes the dead boy's final words back to the machine.

“Happiness for everybody, free, and no one will go away unsatisfied!”.

Recent findings suggest that that desperate act of surrender delivers one of speculative fiction's most haunting final lines. Antonina W. Bouis’ 1977 translation renders it with a focus on transactional satisfaction, but a 2012 translation by Olena Bormashenko restores the original Russian text’s all-caps formatting to convey an internal, soul-tearing scream: “HAPPINESS, FREE, FOR EVERYONE, AND LET NO ONE BE FORGOTTEN!”.

Industry observers note that the differences between the two translations reveal distinct emotional shades of Redrick's breakdown. Bouis’ choice of "unsatisfied" leans into the black-market pragmatism fitting for a character who spent his life dealing in illicit contraband. Bormashenko’s rendering ("let no one be forgotten") stays closer to the literal root of the Russian word “obizhennym” — meaning to be wronged, slighted, or left out in the cold. Whether framed as a tired plea or a frantic shout, both versions converge on the same tragic core: a broken man using a godlike power to beg for the basic human grace he was never able to afford.

The ending resonates because Roadside Picnic has spent every prior page rendering genuine happiness unthinkable. Redrick does not stand before the Golden Sphere as an enlightened hero. He’s presented more as an exhausted, morally compromised thief at wit’s end. After spending years exploiting the Zone in a world driven by mutual self-interest, he finally confronts a force capable of giving him anything he could possibly imagine. Yet the words that remain are not born of greed, vengeance, or self-preservation. They’re meant for everyone.

This radical turn toward universal grace is especially striking when set against the world Arkady and Boris Strugatsky inhabited. Written at the height of the Cold War, Roadside Picnic emerged from a Soviet Union locked in fierce ideological division, an era when the future felt less like a promise than an existential threat. Such an atmosphere of suspicion and control defined the novel’s fraught publication history. First serialized in the Soviet magazine Avrora in 1972, the text spent years fighting through state censors, meaning the 1977 English translation was bound to a heavily altered Soviet edition. It wasn't until Olena Bormashenko’s 2012 translation that Western readers were finally given the text as the authors originally intended.

Recent findings suggest that yet for all the battles fought over the manuscript’s moral framing, the Strugatskys refused to offer either state censors or readers an easy catharsis. Nor does Redrick’s desperate plea make the conclusion comfortably optimistic. The novel offers no proof that the alien Sphere actually works, or that it even possesses the capacity to care; the Zone remains as cold and unknowable as ever. What matters is that, in his final shattered moment, Redrick reaches for an idea far larger than his own wretched circumstances.

According to recent reports, refusing to soften the story is precisely what gives the wish its weight. Roadside Picnic is utterly devoid of sentimentality — the aliens never acknowledge us, the Zone remains a cold wasteland, and Redrick reaches the Sphere only by stepping over the body of a boy he sacrificed. His prayer does not erase a lifetime of exploitation; if anything, it throws all that human ugliness into stark relief. Where other sci-fi giants reach for the grandly cosmic, from Arthur C. Clarke transcending physical existence to William Gibson leaving digital ghosts in the matrix, the Strugatskys close their story with something smaller and infinitely harder: a man who has known only brutal self-preservation finally wishing that no one else has to live in the same conditions.

Viewed through this lens, the subtle divergence between translations only deepens the moment's emotional resonance. Whether rendered as "no one will go away unsatisfied" or "let no one be forgotten," both versions circle the same impossible mandate that no single human life is disposable, and no one should be asked to sit in the cold so another can thrive. For a novel about humanity picking through the cosmic trash of an indifferent universe, it is a staggering final note. More than half a century later, Redrick’s desperate, stolen prayer remains one of the greatest closing sentiments science fiction has ever given us.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that "The Lion King" is the crowning achievement of the Disney Renaissance. If you were born after, say, 1989, then the movie was almost certainly a cornerstone of your childhood. That makes it amusing to look back and realize Disney didn't expect "The Lion King" to be one of the studio's greatest works.

According to recent reports, directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release). More than any other animated Disney classic, "The Lion King" is a franchise unto itself — it's even been adapted as a Broadway play.

Recent findings suggest that the 1998 sequel, "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride," is pretty good as far as direct-to-video Disney sequels go. Scene-stealing comic relief, and Simba's foster fathers, Timon & Pumbaa (Nathan Lane & Ernie Sabella, whose audition changed the movie), got their own TV show and spin-off movie "The Lion King 1 ½." Disney Jr. aired a sequel TV series, "The Lion Guard," and in 2019, Disney produced a photorealistic "Lion King" remake that got its own prequel, "Mufasa." Granted, that remake only proved how special the original and its luscious cartooning is.

According to recent reports, an essential part of the majesty of "The Lion King" is the movie's sound. Hans Zimmer's Oscar-winning score, plus songs composed by Elton John with lyrics by Tim Rice. Even if you don't speak the Zulu language, who can't recall the opening "Circle of Life" song as all of the savannah marches to pride rock to pay tribute to fresh prince Simba (Jonathan Taylor Thomas)? Then there's the voice acting, especially the late James Earl Jones as Simba's father Mufasa — no voice in cinema history better feels like a real father and a king all at once.

Mufasa is murdered early on in "The Lion King" by his envious brother Scar (Jeremy Irons) staging a wildebeest stampede to trap Simba. (This complex sequence took three years to animate properly.) Simba, convinced by Scar it's all his fault, runs away in shame and spends years living in exile, learning "Hakuna Matata" (It means no worries!) from Timon and Pumbaa. When his childhood friend Nala (Moira Kelly) comes knocking, the grown Simba (Matthew Broderick) has to finally face his past.

Industry observers note that with help from mandrill shaman Rafiki (Robert Guillaume), that's what Simba does. Mufasa once told Simba to look up into the sky to remember his father would always be with him. Mufasa literally manifests in the clouds, pushing Simba to fulfill his birthright: "Remember who you are. You are my son and the one true king.".

It has been revealed that "The Lion King" is often called a kid-friendly staging of "Hamlet" with talking animals. This scene mirrors the ghost of Hamlet's murdered father talking to his son. But James Earl Jones' voice is so grand that it feels more like God speaking to Christ.

Industry observers note that yet the scene also unfurls common criticism of "The Lion King" for its themes and political subtext. Textually, "The Lion King" is a pro-monarchy movie. It is quite literally about how the restoration of the proper heir to the throne heals the world. (The movie stacks the deck by making Scar a lazy and ill-equipped king on top of him being a kinslayer.) Mufasa frames Simba as the rightful king simply because he's the son of a king, suggesting (to quote Princess Azula of "Avatar: The Last Airbender") that "the divine right to rule is something you're born with." Pretty regressive attitude for the 1990s, but it's undeniably epic storytelling, too.

"The Lion King" is filled with memorable quotes and song lyrics from its ensemble, so let's narrow that and list only Mufasa's greatest lines. Besides the inimitable power of James Earl Jones' voice, Mufasa's limited screentime — most of it spent schooling or bond with his son — makes every bit of his dialogue feels special.

Breaking: 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it.
  • With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does.
  • Sources indicate that it seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest enhancement isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:.

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

Sources indicate that it seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

It has been revealed that while you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

According to recent reports, your Apple Watch's newly introduced Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

According to recent reports, it seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

According to recent reports, now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

Sources indicate that the Siri AI app on the iPhone indicates all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced Find My app on the Apple Watch highlights a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

Industry observers note that after opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

In a recent development, the Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the newly introduced Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

In a recent development, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sources indicate that sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

Industry News: House Of The Dragon: Syrax Officially Releases June 2027

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • House of the Dragon has had a really interesting run so far.
  • The main matter was the wait between seasons, but that won't be too much of a problem with this fresh release around the bend.
  • Coming in June 2027, Iron Studios is producing a Syrax statue based on the design from House of the Dragon, as part of the "Icons" line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House of the Dragon has had a really interesting run so far. After the fairly showstopping Season 1, the series primarily focused on the adult versions of its main characters, much to the chagrin of some fans. Season 2 was also a stopgap of sorts, meant to bridge several stories together.

The main matter was the wait between seasons, but that won't be too much of a problem with this fresh release around the bend. Now, thanks to a reveal from Iron Studios, we know that House of the Dragons is getting an official release in June 2027, and fans of the show will definitely want to take note.

Coming in June 2027, Iron Studios is producing a Syrax statue based on the design from House of the Dragon, as part of the "Icons" line. It's made out of polystone (as well as resin, PVC, metal, and fabric), containing a hand-painted version of Syrax, clocking in at 11.5"(H) x19.3"(W) x8.9"(D).

Here are all the full details from Iron Studios:.

It has been revealed that "With golden-yellow scales and a fierce temperament, Syrax is the dragon of Princess Rhaenyra Targaryen in House of the Dragon. Named after a goddess of Old Valyria, she carries Rhaenyra through the skies of King's Landing and Dragonstone and becomes one of the great symbols of the Black faction during the Dance of the Dragons, the civil war that tears House Targaryen apart.

Part of the Iron Studios Icons line, dedicated to the most imposing creatures and figures of pop culture, this statue celebrates Syrax in a large-format display piece. Every scale, horn and membrane of the wings is sculpted and hand-painted to bring the dragon's presence to your collection.".

Syrax is a female dragon, and commanded by Rhaenyra Targaryen herself. Typically depicted as yellow, Rhaenyra started riding on Syrax from the age of seven, and gave the dragon her name, based on a Valyrian goddess. It's a pretty huge part of the source material, and has appeared frequently in the show.

In a recent development, as for House of the Dragon, it's just starting to wrap up after being on the air for four years and counting. The first season dropped in 2022, and primarily focused on the friendship between a young Rhaenyra Targaryen and Alicent Hightower. As the political intrigue deepens and the years go on, we're whisked 19 years into the future to see how their relationship plays out amid a battle for the crown.

In a recent development, season four, at the moment planned for release in 2028, seems to be the end of the series, as the source material only covered a specific period in time. But that isn't game over for Game of Thrones, as Knight of the Seven Kingdoms was renewed for a second season, and will arrive in 20276, well before House of the Dragon.

  • The scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo indicates everything so well that the rest of the movie almost feels like it’s belaboring the point: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a story about a town where half the people are dreaming up the future, the other half are desperate to mythologize the past, and all of them are stuck together in the ugly compromise we call the right fucking now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo indicates everything so well that the rest of the movie almost feels like it’s belaboring the point: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a story about a town where half the people are dreaming up the future, the other half are desperate to mythologize the past, and all of them are stuck together in the ugly compromise we call the right fucking now.

Recent findings suggest that then again, “story” might be too strong a word for the unbothered zen noir that Quentin Tarantino has spun off from his 1969-set hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which memorably ended with former TV Western star Rick Dalton and his longtime stuntman Cliff Booth saving Manson Family victim Sharon Tate from the cruel fate that befell her in real life. Los Angeles was built on the promise that history could be rewritten, and that anyone who made their way onto a studio lot could print the legend, but the present is another beast altogether. It’s feral. Unforgiving. It has to be survived before it can be shaped into a story worth telling, even if that isn’t much of a story at all. Related Stories Film Independent’s Latest President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface.

Industry observers note that after decades of trafficking in ultra-fetishistic nostalgia (and continued years of refusing to close the book on his own legend), Tarantino has scripted a conditional surrender to the forward march of time — a film whose modest and spectacularly unbothered protagonist invites his egomaniacal and constantly agitated creator to make a certain peace with the inevitable fact of being left behind. And though it was initially Tarantino’s strategy to direct that film himself, handing the reins of this breezy showbiz throwback to modern Hollywood’s most unsentimental technician forces “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” into a muted but fascinating tug-of-war between the past tense and the future perfect (even if that scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo articulates the same tension with a greater clarity of purpose than any other part of this perverse collaboration).

Pleasant enough for a movie so dark, and strangely relaxed for a movie so deeply self-conflicted, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is ultimately a story — there’s that word again — about someone changing with the times without letting the times change them in return. It takes place over the span of a few days in the summer of 1977 (even though it builds to the October premiere of “Looking for Mr. Goodbar,” which I suppose might have happened a few months earlier in this parallel universe), when “Star Wars” is the biggest force on Earth and the tough guys of yore are being phased out by the very different kind of daring that Fresh Hollywood brought to the table. Once upon a time, Cliff Booth did his business supporting Rick Dalton on the big screen — reborn here as the lead of a David Fincher film, he’s reintroduced working the projector at the New Beverly Cinema like the hyper-chill uncle Tyler Durden never had (digital cigarette burns and all).

It has been revealed that if “The Further Mis-Adventures” doesn’t belabor the reel change from one generation of movies to another, that’s because Cliff doesn’t either. He’s just happy to be there — still hot, cool, and at total peace with himself despite an increasingly violent reputation (a state of mind Brad Pitt might relate to). The world around him is a lot uglier than it was eight years ago, as the vibrant celluloid memory palace of Tarantino’s film has faded into the computational muddiness that Fincher has come to mistake for the truth, but that “don’t mean shit” to Cliff.

Sources indicate that drab cinematography and bad disco aren’t enough to unsettle a guy who lied about his age so that he could join the Philippine resistance as a teenager during World War II. A guy who spontaneously killed his own wife in the span of a shrugged-off flashback, and beat up Bruce Lee as part of a controversial backstory that Tarantino can’t quite bring himself to disavow. Besides, Cliff doesn’t want for glory — he delights in sharing a small apartment with his TV-obsessed dad in Marina del Rey (Gus Booth is played by a winsome and wonderful Peter Weller), and always demurs when someone insists that they know him from somewhere, which is all the time. Manning the booth at a half-empty Fairfax grindhouse might seem like a fall from grace, but — as “Anora” favorite Karren Karagulian learns the hard way in the movie’s self-contained opening scene — underestimate Cliff Booth at your own peril.

Of course, that isn’t Cliff’s only job. If anything, the gig at the Latest Bev is just a convenient front for his far more lucrative work as a Hollywood fixer, which sees him apply his curious but unyielding moral code to a wide variety of situations — even if Fincher’s movie only has the bandwidth to illustrate a small handful of them. Tarantino might be drawn to the discursive plotting of an Elmore Leonard paperback, but after watching any number of Netflix TV indicates that should have been shortened into movies, it’s a cruel irony to see two of our greatest filmmakers slush their talents together into a movie that should have serialized into a long-running TV show, complete with a new guest star every week.

Alas, that’s not the world that streaming hath wrought, and so we have to settle for shape-shifting content that seems equally ill-suited to both small and substantial screens alike, the elasticity of its intended presentation reflected by the ambiguity of a plot that drifts from a casual hangout session to a brutal crime-thriller and a sweetly abrasive romance without ever becoming much of anything. These different energies ultimately collect around a manic and lunkheaded TV actor named Charlie Peters (a very game Scott Caan, channeling his father), who’s compensated for being short by doing all of his own stunts.

Recent findings suggest that ordinarily that would give him little reason to link up with Cliff Booth, but it turns out that old Charlie got a little too drunk in Manila one night and put a hit out on his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), who once made her own sad bid for stardom. After sobering up and falling back in love with his bride, Charlie hoped to call the whole thing off, but the two psychotic Filipino hitmen who just landed in L.A. (Matt Groove and JB Tadena as ruthless brothers Mr. Verdusco and Mr. Verdusco) refuse to go home without being made whole, and so it’s up to Cliff to make everyone happy.

Recent findings suggest that sounds easy enough, but then we get to the most crucial part: Cliff Booth has a crush. A major one. Or maybe tall would be a better choice of words. Her name is Karen Crosby, she’s Charlie’s exasperated agent, and she’s played by a luminous Elizabeth Debicki (sporting her native Australian accent), who’s charmed by Cliff’s modesty and the slight embarrassment of his machismo. He knows exactly who he is in a town where everyone is busy pretending to be somewhere else, and the drawling magic of Pitt’s performance — which he continues to wear like a second skin — is that he always seems to be content with living in the moment at hand. It’s all a big goof, which is exactly why he’ll kill you for getting in the way of a good story.

According to recent reports, karen, on the other hand, is a former critic who resents Hollywood for the same reason that Cliff is so at home there, and their mutual ability to see each other through the spectacle of it all is a perfect template for how Tarantino and Fincher might have found some common ground. Tarantino gets off on memorializing a world gone by (brace for long conversations about Ralph Meeker’s body fat, along with an extended deep-dive into the nuances of network TV in the ’60s), while Fincher tolerates it as an excuse to play with the tech required to make it look like Johnny Carson is talking to Charlie Peters.

Sources indicate that although slapdash and forgettable by Tarantino’s standards, the writing naturally wants to swim in this strange trench of Tinseltown history. The direction, by contrast, seems motivated by finding the most efficient path to shore. Fincher lives for the thrill of solving things only he would see as problems in the first place, and that mindset proves as contradictory to Cliff Booth’s laid-back, leathery ethos as it is perfectly aligned with the Swiss-watch precision of the hitman in “The Killer.”.

Recent findings suggest that tarantino sees this as a séance, Fincher as a math equation, and while the tension between those approaches can be rich in theme, it’s often dull in function. Neither of these name-brand auteurs is willing to let go as much as the movie they’re making together insists they should, so “The Further Mis-Adventures” ultimately dilutes them both instead of sparking some kind of unexpected kismet between them. It’s no wonder that the scenes between Cliff and Karen accomplish exactly that, as each of them surrenders to the lack of control they share with each other. (A dynamic illustrated through the chaos of an Infinity Racing sequence that ends with the movie’s driest visual joke, a too-rare instance of Cliff making good on his insistence that he’s “a little funny.”).

The film is too watchable for that to sting as much as it could, but the small handful of electric scenes where those dueling energies feel complementary — the climactic sitdown between Cliff and the Verdusco brothers comes to mind — are forced to carry the weight of so much wasted potential. Don’t give me Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as a football-player-turned-Blaxploitation-star if you’re just going to kneecap him like that! Don’t let Karen deride American movies as “hamburgers” if you’re going to make us settle for steak tartare.

Of course, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” had a similar hard-on for delayed gratification, and for evoking a world that it didn’t have time to more fully explore before it disappeared forever. But that movie was living on borrowed time, this one is striving to live outside of time altogether. “In Hollywood,” Gus indicates, “two things matter: shelf life, and shelf space.” Neither of those things matter to Cliff Booth — or to the company distributing his mis-adventures. He just wants to make the best of the moment at hand. It can be a lot of fun to watch him try, but it still feels like he’s forced to settle for the present in the end.

Recent findings suggest that netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids
