📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications.
  • The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe.
  • Sources indicate that openAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

Sources indicate that openAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for owners is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Sources indicate that accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly indicates that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says customers accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Industry observers note that gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health complications like eating disorders.

Recent findings suggest that these protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

Sources indicate that as with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly swiftly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

According to recent reports, apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

According to recent reports, the new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of owners, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. People must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

It has been revealed that if you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

In a recent development, parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft indicates consumers identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence.".

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires customers to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide owners towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the substantial seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

According to recent reports, with today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a upcoming feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Industry observers note that previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the newly introduced face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

It has been revealed that after updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

Industry News: 6 Funniest Far Side Comics Starring the Devil

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the 1980s and 1990s, nothing in the funny pages was quite as dark as The Far Side.
  • Meanwhile, The Far Side featured jokes about hangings and murder — death was a regular punchline.
  • In this comic from June 11, 1988, a pizza gets delivered to Hell and Satan is clearly unhappy about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the 1980s and 1990s, nothing in the funny pages was quite as dark as The Far Side. Lucy van Pelt pulling the football away from Charlie Brown as he was about to kick it is about as dark as things got in Peanuts. And in Garfield, the lazy cat’s darkest running gag also revolved around a kick — when he’d kick Odie the dog off a table.

Meanwhile, The Far Side featured jokes about hangings and murder — death was a regular punchline. Larson also liked to make light of whatever came after death. Occasionally he’d make a joke about Heaven, but he clearly found Hell far more amusing. Many Far Side comics take place in the underworld — or some specific version of it — with Satan a recurring figure in his comic strips. Few characters in The Far Side appeared more than once, but the Devil himself made many appearances.

In this comic from June 11, 1988, a pizza gets delivered to Hell and Satan is clearly unhappy about it. “First of all, this is going straight back — and I’ll just have a little chat with whoever placed the order,” says Satan. The best little detail in the comic strip is the slogan on the pizza box. It says “Jerry’s Pizza: We Deliver Anywhere” and Jerry clearly lives up to her word.

I can understand the Devil’s annoyance. Pizza is one of the greatest pleasures on Earth, which means that pizza is absolutely disqualified from being served in Hell, even though there’s a perfect-looking pizza oven literally everywhere you look.

In a recent development, A recurring source of humor in Gary Larson’s comic strip was to take a common phrase or idiom and interpret it as literally as possible. In one comic from 1992, he picked apart the common phrase “ride off into the sunset” by depicting a burnt-up cowboy that had literally ridden into the sun. In another comic from 1985, he played on the phrase “dressed to kill” by showing two sharks in fancy evening attire.

Industry observers note that in this comic from 1982, Larson dissected the phrase “To Hell and back” by turning Hell into a mere tourist destination. In it, a man is showing off slides from his vacation, which include a picture of his wife standing with the Devil. Especially fun here is how happy the Devil is, while the man’s wife looks bored by the encounter.

Recent findings suggest that while Hell showed up in several Far Side comics, it wasn’t always the same Hell, or at least it didn’t appear to be. Several comic strips depicted very specific, different forms of Hell, each of which was specifically designed to torture a particular resident of the underworld. For example, this comic from 1990 has the caption “Bowler’s Hell.” It shows the bowler having made an impossible-to-hit split, with the Devil saying “Whoa! Another split?... What a bummer!” Clearly, endless splits like this would be the worst possible punishment for a bowler.

If a bowler’s version of Hell is endless splits, a classical conductor's version of Hell would have to be an orchestra filled only with banjos. Larson seemingly found banjos to be obnoxious instruments as a number of his comic strips feature them in a less-than-flattering light. In another, more Earthly Far Side comic, a different conductor is horrified by the sound of a banjo in his orchestra as he shouts “Stop! Stop! What’s that sound? What’s that sound?”.

Still, it seems that, for Gary Larson’s musical tastes, banjos rank higher than accordions, which received even harsher treatment.

According to recent reports, this Far Side comic contrasts Heaven and Hell. In Heaven, you receive a harp when you die, but in Hell, the instrument given out to all upcoming inhabitants is an accordion. I seriously wonder if any accordion or banjo players were ever offended by Gary Larson’s repeated attacks on their instruments.

In yet another specific version of Hell, dogs who have been sentenced to eternal damnation are forced to work as their arch-nemesis: mailmen. Originally, I’d assumed that this comic strip was a parody of the movie All Dogs Go to Heaven, a truly beautiful animated film directed by Don Bluth. But the years don’t add up as this comic strip comes from 1986 while All Dogs Go to Heaven is from 1989.

And while I’m not the kind of person to get into a theological debate between any two parties, I think Don Bluth is right about where dogs go in the afterlife, whereas Larson is totally wrong about any dog going to hell.

8 Most Suspenseful Thriller Movies of All Time, Ranked

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Feel free to connect with him or check out his work.
  • According to recent reports, there’s no single definition of a great thriller.
  • In a recent development, when a film leaves the viewers desperate to know what happens next, that’s when it’s doing something right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

According to recent reports, there’s no single definition of a great thriller. However, what most of them have in common is a sense of tension. Now, the way this tension is created can vary dramatically from film to film. Some thrillers build suspense through psychological mind games, while others rely on shocking twists that completely reframe the narrative in a single moment. A memorable thriller doesn’t just surprise the audience, though — it traps them, makes them question everything, and refuses to play by any rules.

In a recent development, when a film leaves the viewers desperate to know what happens next, that’s when it’s doing something right. Over the years, filmmakers have approached countless ways to build this tension, but only a few have truly mastered it. This is a list of eight such suspenseful thrillers that know exactly when to tighten the noose.

In a recent development, anatomy of a Fall is an intense, entertaining take on the courtroom drama. The film, directed by Justine Triet, opens with a man being found dead outside his remote chalet in the French Alps. His wife, Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller), insists it was an accident or possibly suicide. However, as the investigation unfolds, small inconsistencies lead to the case escalating into a courtroom trial where every detail of the couple’s marriage is called into question. Their visually impaired son, Daniel (Milo Machado-Graner), is the only real witness to the events surrounding his father’s death, which complicates things even more. Anatomy of a Fall is structured like an intricate puzzle where every new piece of information complicates the situation.

In a recent development, however, the procedural format never takes away from the gravity of Sandra and her husband’s fractured relationship. Hüller delivers an extraordinary performance, and her character’s emotional ambiguity is what fuels the narrative. This results in a story that isn’t merely about solving a crime. Instead, Anatomy of a Fall dissects the fragile dynamics of marriage, resentment, and grief. By the time the trial concludes, the audience is left with a lingering sense of doubt. The film builds suspense through uncertainty instead of relying on traditional twists or grand reveals. This layered, human approach is what makes it such a compelling thriller.

David Fincher’s The Game is the perfect example of a well-executed thriller. The film stars Michael Douglas as a wealthy but emotionally detached investment banker, Nicholas Van Orton, living in San Francisco, who receives an unusual gift from his estranged brother Conrad (Sean Penn) on his 48th birthday. The gift in question is an invitation to participate in an elaborate entertainment experience, known as a “game,” run by a mysterious organization called Consumer Recreation Services. At first, Nicholas assumes it’s just a harmless distraction. However, things take a turn when strange things start happening in his everyday life. As the game intensifies, Nicholas finds TV broadcasts speaking directly to him, people start following him, his business reputation is threatened, and his money starts vanishing.

The film then becomes a masterclass in paranoia and unpredictability, where the protagonist stops trusting anyone and is constantly questioning his reality. What’s genuinely heartbreaking is when he learns that his alliance with a waitress named Christine (Deborah Kara Unger) might also be a part of the game. However, this kind of shock is exactly why The Game is such an effective thriller. Fincher creates a destabilizing experience for both Nicholas and the audience, which makes every twist feel unsettling but plausible at the same time. This growing sense of tension makes the final reveal land with absolute perfection, solidifying The Game as one of the most suspenseful thrillers of all time.

No list of suspense thrillers would ever be complete without this Alfred Hitchcock masterpiece. Rear Window has to be one of the director’s most influential works and proves just why he was known as the “Master of Suspense.” The film follows photojournalist L.B. “Jeff” Jefferies (James Stewart), who is stuck in his Greenwich Village apartment with a broken leg after a dangerous assignment. To kill time, Jeff begins watching his neighbors across the courtyard through his rear window. However, his harmless curiosity turns into something far more dangerous when one of them begins to stand out for all the wrong reasons. Lars Thorwald (Raymond Burr) is a traveling salesman who lives with his wife, who is often sick. Jeff notices him making several late-night trips carrying a suitcase, soon after which his wife mysteriously disappears.

It has been revealed that the more Jeff watches, the more convinced he is that Thornwald has murdered her with the help of his girlfriend Lisa Fremont (Grace Kelly) and nurse Stella (Thelma Ritter). That kicks off an investigation based entirely on observation. Jeff can’t leave his wheelchair, so he relies on binoculars and instincts to piece together what really happened. Hitchcock places the audience in the same position as Jeff and restricts them to his confined perspective. This brilliant setup heightens every little movement and conversation and makes the viewers feel like active participants in this baffling mystery. Rear Window remains just as gripping decades later and proves that a great thriller doesn’t need to rely on spectacle to leave an impact.

Zodiac is another Fincher thriller that remains the benchmark for the genre. The film turns one of America’s most infamous unsolved crimes into a cinematic experience that stays with the audience long after the credits roll. The story follows the real-life manhunt for the Zodiac Killer, who terrorized the San Francisco Bay Area in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The film unfolds through the perspectives of three men whose lives become consumed by the case: political cartoonist Robert Graysmith (Jake Gyllenhaal), crime reporter Paul Avery (Robert Downey Jr.), and homicide inspector Dave Toschi (Mark Ruffalo). Graysmith, in particular, becomes increasingly fascinated by the killer’s cryptic letters to the police and newspapers and begins an investigation of his own to decode them.

However, this curiosity slowly turns into an obsession and pushes Graysmith into a web of complicated clues that seem to lead nowhere. The film explores how the case takes a toll on everyone involved and attempts to center the story on the painful process of investigation itself. Zodiac isn’t really interested in finding who the killer is and deliberately avoids the usual beats a crime thriller would typically follow. The tension here comes from watching these people chase lead after lead, only to end up with nothing. That lingering uncertainty makes the climax all the more shocking. Zodiac mirrors the frustration that defined the real mystery of the killer and perfectly captures the psychological toll of it all.

It has been revealed that hitchcock’s Psycho is just one of those films that never get old. In fact, it remains a defining moment in the evolution of modern horror and thriller storytelling. The story begins with Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) impulsively stealing $40,000 from her employer and going on the run in hopes of starting a new life with her boyfriend. During her drive, she runs into a terrible storm and decides to pull over at the quiet roadside Bates Motel. The establishment is run by the polite but socially awkward Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins), who lives in a giant Victorian house overlooking the property with his overbearing mother. The story plays out like a traditional crime drama centered on Marion before Hitchcock subverts all expectations, and the audience witnesses her shocking murder in the now-iconic shower scene.

In a recent development, as Marion’s sister Lila (Vera Miles) and boyfriend Sam Loomis (John Gavin) begin searching for her, the investigation slowly leads them back to the eerie motel and the secrets hidden inside Norman’s house. The narrative unfolds slowly, and the audience gradually uncovers that the motel owner is far more complicated and terrifying than he initially seems. Perkins’s performance definitely deserves a mention here because his portrayal of Norman is the heart of the film. That’s exactly what makes the final reveal and Norman’s eventual descent into madness land so perfectly. Looking back, the brilliance of Psycho lies in how carefully the director builds up to that one moment, and it is the reason why the film has stood the test of time.

The Silence of the Lambs is undisputedly one of the greatest psychological thrillers ever made. The film follows FBI trainee Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster), who is tasked with helping track down a brutal serial killer known as Buffalo Bill (Ted Levine). Now, to understand the mind of a killer, Clarice is sent to interview imprisoned psychiatrist and cannibalistic murderer Dr. Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins). The catch is that Lecter only agrees to offer clues about Buffalo Bill if Clarice reveals deeply personal details about her own past to him. This uneasy dynamic is the center of the story as Clarice pieces together fragments of information about Buffalo Bill’s disturbing motives while navigating her strange relationship with Lecter.

Their conversations feel like a cat-and-mouse game where Lecter is constantly trying to manipulate and analyze Clarice’s fears. On the other hand, Buffalo Bill continues abducting women, which raises the stakes of the investigation and pushes the FBI trainee to rely on Lecter’s transactional guidance. The film builds suspense by focusing on its characters and their psychology. The horror is rooted in the conversations between Clarice and Lecter rather than momentary shocks. The Silence of the Lambs is a must-watch for anyone who appreciates the art of a slow burn.

Shutter Island marked a turning point for modern era psychological thrillers. The film, adapted from Dennis Lehane’s 2003 novel of the same name, is set on an eerie, remote island that houses a psychiatric hospital for the criminally insane. The story follows U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo) as they arrive on the island to investigate the disappearance of Rachel Solando, a patient who drowned her three children and somehow vanished from her locked hospital ward. Things only get stranger from there; when Teddy begins questioning doctors and patients, he realizes that everyone at the hospital is hiding something. Meanwhile, Teddy starts experiencing disturbing migraines, flashbacks, and extremely vivid dreams about his late wife, who died in a tragic fire.

All of this leads him to believe that something sinister is happening on the island, and he is entangled in rumors of secret experiments and impossible conspiracies. However, every conversation and clue pushes him further into a state of confusion. After a while, both Teddy and the audience begin to question what is real and what might just be an illusion. The film slowly builds up to what is easily one of the most memorable plot twists Hollywood has ever seen — one that completely recontextualizes the entire story. Ultimately, Shutter Island revolves around a man who is gradually confronting the darkest corners of his own mind. It’s a psychological puzzle that gets better with every rewatch and never loses its thrill.

Sources indicate that seven might just be one of the darkest thrillers Fincher has ever delivered. The film is unsettling from the get-go, and it refuses to offer the audience or its characters any respite. The story follows veteran detective William Somerset (Morgan Freeman) and his new partner David Mills (Brad Pitt) as they chase a serial killer whose crimes are inspired by the seven deadly sins. Things kick off with a disturbing murder scene where an obese man has been forced to eat until he dies, a crime that represents gluttony. When another victim is discovered with the words “greed” marked at the crime scene, Somerset realizes this is the work of an extremely methodical killer operating with a twisted moral compass.

What makes Seven such a compelling movie is the interesting dynamic between the thoughtful and patient Somerset and the younger, much more impulsive Mills, who grows increasingly frustrated as the killer keeps getting away. The film’s final act is what cements Seven as an unforgettable experience as the antagonist (Kevin Spacey) reveals that he committed the sin of envy and delivers that now-infamous Box to Mills. Seven ends on a devastating note that leaves everyone shaken because, despite everything, the killer’s proposal works exactly as he intended. This bleak storytelling and relentless sense of dread make Seven a masterclass in suspense.

Fans of “The Gilded Age,” rejoice! There are still more luncheons to plan, more balls to savor, and more opera opening nights to fight over. Yes, the HBO original series has been renewed for a fifth season.

The move follows a surge in popularity that began with the show’s drama-filled third season, which saw Bertha (Carrie Coon) and George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) relationship strain, and has continued with the fourth season, which has dealt with their marriage troubles, the wedding of Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), and a visit from Grover Cleveland.

Clearly, it’s working. Viewership for Season 4 has grown week over week, HBO stated in a press release. Episode 3 hit a season high of 4.3 million U.S. cross-platform viewers and episodes are averaging 5.9 million viewers and growing. That outpaces the prior season by nearly 20 percent. Related Stories ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story.

According to recent reports, the turnaround is striking because “The Gilded Age” was very much on the bubble for most of its first two seasons. Bringing 19th-century high-society to life is expensive, and the show initially struggled to become a ratings powerhouse despite being co-created by Julian Fellowes of “Downton Abbey” fame. In interviews, the cast admitted that they often feared they would be canceled. But audiences have shown up in a big way, and Fellowes and his co-creator Sonja Warfield recently told IndieWire that they have more stories to tell beyond this season.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”.

In its three eligible seasons, “The Gilded Age” has earned 15 total Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Drama Series and Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, as well as a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

“The Gilded Age” cast includes Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Louisa Jacobson, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Blake Ritson, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, and Kristine Nielsen.

“The Gilded Age” is a co-production between HBO and Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:.

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

It has been revealed that at this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication challenges impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't mentioned what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for people of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Book adaptations of acclaimed sci-fi books are not always bound to succeed.
  • It has been revealed that the show in question, Silo, is based on Hugh Howey's book trilogy of the same name.
  • With season 3, Apple TV's Silo takes massive creative liberties from the very beginning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Book adaptations of acclaimed sci-fi books are not always bound to succeed. While some TV adaptations follow their source material a little too closely, others drift too far away and end up telling completely different stories. One sci-fi show on Apple TV, however, strikes the rare balance between the two and perfectly captures its source material's essence by carefully rewriting it for the screen.

It has been revealed that the show in question, Silo, is based on Hugh Howey's book trilogy of the same name. In season 1, Silo covers a significant chunk of the original novel series' first book, Wool. While at it, it slightly changes the book's tone and turns into a grand post-apocalyptic conspiracy thriller. Silo season 2 then goes on to introduce even bigger book changes, adding immense political intrigue to the original story.

With season 3, Apple TV's Silo takes massive creative liberties from the very beginning. For obvious reasons, many fans of Hugh Howey's original Silo books were not too content with these. In hindsight, however, Apple TV's Silo comes off as a masterclass in book adaptations as it delivers peak science fiction in every episode.

It has been revealed that the foundation of Silo's story rests in Plato's Allegory of the Cave. In the original allegory, prisoners in a cave mistake shadows on a wall for reality until one of them finally escapes into the sun. A similar game of lies and deception keeps the characters of Silo trapped in an underground city until Rebecca Ferguson's Juliette ends up going out and finding the truth.

Recent findings suggest that silo's parallels with Hobbes’s Leviathan emerge when the show highlights the nature of authoritarian control in its story. The fear of seeking knowledge and freedom is so deeply instilled in the silo's citizens across generations through memory-altering drugs, rigid rules of Silo's Pact, and historical revision that they hold obedience synonymous to survival.

According to recent reports, even the overarching surveillance in Silo draws from Bentham and Foucault’s Panopticon. The higher authorities in the show do not have access to large armies to prevent the citizens from leaving. Instead, power is kept secretive and internalized through processes like "The Cleaning" in Silo, without the people knowing that they are contantly being watched and controlled.

Every main character in Silo is also forced to go through the Cartesian crisis as they navigate and accept the harsh truths of their post-apocalyptic world. From Tim Robbins' Bernard to Steve Zahn's Solo, every character is eventually forced to wonder whether anything they have been taught to believe is real. With this, Rene Descartes' "I think, therefore I am" becomes the driver of every character's journey.

In its three-season runtime, so far, Apple TV's Silo has ensured that even aspect of its post-apocalyptic world feels real. The early seasons made one question why the silos did not have elevators and any modern technology. Answers to these eventually emerged, revealing how the lack of elevators and technology is just another means of establishing control and fixed heirarchy inside the silo.

Industry observers note that the world of Silo is packed with many such details that conrete and logical answers. Although Apple TV's Silo suffers from pacing challenges time and again, the show makes up for these shortcomings with its meticulous world-building. In season 3, it even ties its central apocalypse to a major past conspiracy while introducing everything from killer drones to nanobots.

It has been revealed that silo is also all set to end its run on a high and conclusive note in season 4. If its home stretch lands the ending, which it likely will, Silo will cement itself as one Apple TV best sci-fi offerings and one of the greatest dystopian sci-fi indicates of the 21st century.

In a dystopian future, men and women reside in a vast underground silo governed by strict regulations, believed to shield them from the hazardous world above. The series delves into the complex social order within the silo and the mysteries surrounding their subterranean existence.

72 Years Later, Lord of the Rings Officially Reveals Why Sauron Is So Evil

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sauron is one of the most famous villains of all time, but The Lord of the Rings doesn’t really explore why the Dark Lord is so obsessed with conquering all of Middle-earth.
  • Industry observers note that sauron is sometimes called the Great Deceiver, and his morality has seemingly shifted along with his face.
  • The humiliation not only changed his appearance but seemingly made Sauron rethink his outlook and regret some of his past misdeeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sauron is one of the most famous villains of all time, but The Lord of the Rings doesn’t really explore why the Dark Lord is so obsessed with conquering all of Middle-earth. The prequel series The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power has been working to make Sauron (Charlie Vickers) more complex — which isn’t hard since he gets to have conversations with other characters rather than solely appear as an ominous eye. He’s a master of deception who has appeared in multiple guises to further his schemes, but in one of the latest episodes released Wednesday, Sauron gets honest and reveals his true motivations.

Industry observers note that sauron is sometimes called the Great Deceiver, and his morality has seemingly shifted along with his face. He is a Maia, a cosmic being created to serve Aulë, the divine smith revered by the dwarves. But Sauron began working for the fallen Valar Morgoth and followed him to Middle-earth to serve as his chief lieutenant. When Morgoth was defeated, Sauron tried to take control of his Orc armies. Instead, Adar (Joseph Mawle), an Elf tortured and twisted by Morgoth and Sauron into becoming the progenitor of the Orcs, killed Sauron with Morgoth’s crown. It took Sauron a thousand years to put himself back together.

The humiliation not only changed his appearance but seemingly made Sauron rethink his outlook and regret some of his past misdeeds. He traveled with a group of refugees fleeing Orcs and was convinced that choosing to do good every day might make up for the evil he had done in the past. But when the refugees were attacked at sea, Sauron didn’t help. He betrayed a man that had been kind to him and stole an heirloom to create a cover story that positioned him as the lost king of the Southlands.

That deception allows him to act on his true motivations, which he reveals in season 3, episode 6, “From Valinor.” Sauron is obsessed with discovering how the Elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) created the Elven rings, and believes he can learn the secret from Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), who was imprisoned next to the last of the Elven smiths. Threatened with torture, Celeborn asks Sauron why he’s trying to master the rings and remake the world.

“It will bring me bliss,” Sauron responds. “I have lived a thousand lifetimes, and existence has but one true joy that is god to all others: To know, to feel the moment, the precise instant another being submits his or her will to yours. There is no greater pleasure, and I shall have it with all, for always.”.

Celeborn is disgusted that Sauron has unleashed so much suffering because it makes him feel good, but the Dark Lord responds with a smile, “That is the only reason any free being has ever done anything.”.

Sauron repeatedly demonstrates the sadistic pleasure he takes from getting people to give in to his wishes. He gives Celeborn a little smirk when he states “or her,” clearly thinking of how he seduced Celeborn’s wife Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and persuaded her to proclaim him a king and introduce him to Celebrimbor. While disguised as a servant of the Valar called Annatar, Sauron deceived Celebrimbor into helping him make more rings, a mistake that eventually led to the smith’s death and the destruction of the Elven city Eregion.

Industry observers note that celebrimbor’s body hangs in Sauron’s workshop and an apparition of the dead elf has appeared to Sauron throughout this season, taunting the would-be Dark Lord that the knowledge needed to master the Elven rings and Galadriel will forever elude his grasp. Sauron is infuriated that Celebrimbor would keep secrets from him, but Celebrimbor explains that they were never truly partners. “The machinery of your soul is missing a piece, the one that allows for a true bond, a true union with another being,” he indicates. “So in place of connection you seek control.”.

Recent findings suggest that whether or not this version of Celebrimbor is just a figment of Sauron’s imagination, he’s certainly right. Sauron is unable to gain bliss from love or friendship, the forces that fuel the heroes of Middle-earth such as Frodo, Aragorn, and Sam. Instead, Sauron seeks to crush the wills of those around him. He forces his future Ring-servants to fight to the death for a chance at power. He poisons an Elf prisoner to convince her husband to give him information about the rogue Orc Marnûkh (Adam Young), then denies him the antidote he promised. He persuades Marnûkh to give him information to spare his children, and then reveals that they’ve already been killed.

“From Valinor” ends with the culmination of Sauron’s looks for Celeborn. After being brutally tortured and returned to his cell, Celeborn is seemingly rescued by Galadriel. Giddy with relief, he spills the secret he has been keeping — that he knows Celebrimbor used gold and silver from Valinor to make the Elven rings. Galadriel leans in to kiss her husband, eyes tearing with relief, but as the two embrace, Sauron reveals his deception. “And I thought it was bliss when Galadriel submitted to my will,” he claims, caressing Celeborn. Not only did he get the pleasure of breaking Celeborn, Sauron is also one step closer to his master blueprint of crafting the One Ring that will allow him to finally control all of Middle-earth.

I don’t think I was supposed to hear Anthony Ippolito when he exclaimed, “20 minutes?” right before this interview, as he was given the amount of time this interview would last. Though, it kind of hit me, if you’re not used to doing interviews — and there’s no way Ippolito can be at this young stage of his career — 20 minutes is a long time to make conversation with a total stranger. Especially, as he is quick to point out, after a barrage of quick, three-minute interviews.

Ippolito has been in films and television before — kind of famously now, he played Al Pacino in “The Offer” — but none of those were roles in which he’d have to do press. Let alone playing the lead role in a major motion picture in which everyone wants to talk to him. Oh, and that lead role is as … Sylvester Stallone. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards.

In “I Play Rocky,” yes, Ippolito plays Stallone at the make or break point in Stallone’s career. Stallone had written “Rocky,” a very in-demand script. Not in demand was the idea of Stallone playing Rocky — as MGM offers more and more money to Stallone in an effort to get him to not play Rocky. (If you don’t know, Stallone stuck to his guns, played Rocky, and is now a very wealthy and famous actor.).

Directed by Peter Farrelly, Ippolito says he sent in multiple tapes trying to land this role — which does seem to be in the same spirit as the film itself. Though, Ippolito remarked, when he was actually going through the casting process, that’s not at all what he was thinking, even though it may seem that way now.

Ahead, he tells us (yes, over the course of 20 minutes) the Stallone movies he used to prep for playing Stallone, what is was like to talk to Stallone before filming, and why he loves Stallone and Dolly Parton together in “Rhinestone.” Also, if he had to play Stallone again in another movie, he does have another “I Play” installment in mind….

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You seem excited about this being 20 minutes?

It’s a little strange, I’ve been having three-minute increment conversations with somebody. So, yes, I am excited.

According to recent reports, OK, so how many Stallone movies did you watch? Did you stick to that era? His voice kind of evolves by the late ‘80s.

Yeah, I really tried to stay focused on a period of time. I don’t know the exact number. More so, from the stuff I was looking at I was watching it over and over again, rewatching. With the exception of a few.

Well, “Rocky Balboa.” It’s one of the best movies of the franchise.

For people who haven’t seen that one in a while, it’s very sweet.

In a recent development, it really is. It really is. And he does some excellent work in it. And I think it’s really powerful that he was able to come back many years later, after the fifth one, and make this incredible movie.

From closer to the “Rocky” era, I kind of love him in “The Prisoner of Second Avenue.” Jack Lemmon thinks he stole his wallet….

It’s just scene after scene of Jack Lemmon chasing Stallone through Central Park trying to get his wallet back….

But then Jack Lemmon realizes he left his wallet at home and wound up being the one who mugged Stallone.

But he was mistaken for a mugger and this was part of his glitch, right?

It has been revealed that it’s funny watching it now, because it’s so obviously Sylvester Stallone. So it’s amusing the whole role is just him being chased.

I agree with you and I found that throughout a lot of the stuff I was unearthing throughout this process.

In that, if he hadn’t become famous, I’d still look at him and think, “what an interesting looking dude,” and wonder what happened to him.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of that, there were times during “I Play Rocky,” knowing full well what happens in real life, and I’m still like, “Maybe just take the money. That’s a lot.”.

It’s really remarkable. Especially when you convert the amount from what it was then to what it would be now.

Yeah, I mean … it was difficult to come up with that part of it. According to recent reports, oh, there was more than one? You just kept going?

It has been revealed that and historically Stallone never does that. I say that sarcastically because I’m well aware he has a specific vision for any movie he’s involved in….

Industry observers note that right. Right. So, Stallone went back after that and told somebody he has no idea about it. What was that like? Was he in good spirits or was he apprehensive?

So, I was just really, really excited to meet him and to listen to him. He was really, really generous and disarming and very willing to share what that period of time was like for him.

He then walked off and I thought, “You know, good enough.”.

Very different movies. Well, I like that, You can go in so many different directions. And I appreciate directors and filmmakers who are singular.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before the arrival of Netflix’s Jenna Ortega vehicle Wednesday, the streaming service offered an earlier reboot of a classic ‘90s fantasy franchise, and its comparatively lengthy run highlighted the biggest problem with modern streaming highlights. As the wait for Stranger Things season 4 crept closer to a three-year gap back in 2022, Netflix prepared for the show’s eventual ending with a new, equally massive, nostalgic, and family-friendly replacement franchise.

It has been revealed that while the Stranger Things franchise started out dark and mature and gradually grew more PG-rated as the show’s audience got bigger, Netflix’s replacement series was far more family-friendly from the start. The Addams Family re-imagining Wednesday saw director Tim Burton offer his spin on the famous franchise, borrowing liberally from the live-action Addams Family movies of the ‘90s but shifting the show’s focus to Jenna Ortega’s titular deadpan heroine.

Thanks to a superb performance from Ortega, Wednesday became the colossal success that Netflix hoped for. However, as the wait for Wednesday season 3 continues, it is clear that there are cracks in the show’s formula. Outside a strong cast, the Addams Family reboot isn’t entirely sure of its target audience, has a wonky, uneven tone, and drags out its central mysteries. Moreover, Netflix’s earlier hit Chilling Adventures of Sabrina was a strikingly similar alternative that already addressed these complications in its longer run.

It has been revealed that originally developed by Riverdale creator Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa for the CW, but moved to Netflix midway through the show’s pre-production, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina was conceived as a spinoff of Aguirre-Sacasa's earlier teen show. While Chilling Adventures of Sabrina shares its main character and basic premise with the classic ‘90s children’s show Sabrina the Teenage Witch, the darker, more mature Netflix series was adapted from Aguirre-Sacasa’s subversive Archie Comics series of the same name.

Sources indicate that chilling Adventures of Sabrina began as a magic high school show akin to The Vampire Diaries spinoff Legacies, Wednesday, or Disney’s recent copycat show Coven Academy. However, as the series continued, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina offered viewers some daring experimental storylines that saw the supernatural fantasy series extend its tendrils beyond the world of witches and demons by introducing Lovecraftian Elder Gods and existential stakes.

Chilling Adventures of Sabrina was essentially the same show as Wednesday, except the earlier Netflix series released 36 episodes in the span of two years, and this allowed the show to explore more exciting, unpredictable plots than the later, markedly safer Addams Family reboot. It has since become increasingly common for major streaming shows to take long hiatuses between seasons, meaning viewers have received only 16 episodes of Wednesday in the last four years.

The fact that Chilling Adventures of Sabrina’s two-season, four-part run released more than twice as many episodes as Wednesday in half as much time is not merely a question of quantity over quality. Like Wednesday, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina was a glossy, critically acclaimed fantasy series with expensive effects, a celebrated ensemble cast, ambitious serialized plots, and high production values.

No show that attempts to adapt the works of HP Lovecraft, no matter how tongue-in-cheek it might be, does so without putting a serious budget behind the endeavor. Thus, Chilling Adventures of Sabrina’s 36-episode run instead serves to highlight just how much streaming has changed in the years since the COVID-19 pandemic ended the show’s production in 2020.

It has been revealed that after Stranger Things introduced three-year waits between seasons of streaming indicates, this was adopted as a new normal, and expensive productions like The Rings of Power regularly featured waits of two or more years between seasons. While there is an increasing backlash against this practice, which might explain the humdrum reception of Wednesday season 2 part 2, it will be a long time before viewers can expect to see streaming shows return to Chilling Adventures of Sabrina’s prolific output rate.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers.
  • Recent findings suggest that google notes it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web.
  • Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the firm discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Recent findings suggest that google notes it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a fresh service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google released the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

Industry observers note that it’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

Sources indicate that but perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that owners want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the manufacturer hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

Industry observers note that there isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Sources indicate that finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

  • When Apple first unveiled Face ID, the firm talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.
  • Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….
  • In a recent development, the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Apple first unveiled Face ID, the firm talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….

In a recent development, the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Sources indicate that meantime, in 2017 Apple released Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the organization is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

It has been revealed that I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:.

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

It has been revealed that for myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

Sources indicate that there’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Right now, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook customers have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

It has been revealed that what’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

#4183. Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles
