Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics.
  • American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong.
  • From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “Heat” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds, was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.” Related Stories Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Major Break ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors.

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.).

Early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

Sources indicate that the first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

According to recent reports, in “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.”.

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”.

A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating highlights up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

It’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it substantial and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

Industry observers note that so why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that noted he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Recent findings suggest that then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

According to recent reports, goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt noted he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

On the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

It has been revealed that DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

It has been revealed that the experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

Burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google introduced Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful newly introduced feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is at the moment open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Industry observers note that plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

It has been revealed that ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google indicates this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

Recent findings suggest that if you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Upgrade: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

It has been revealed that supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build latest production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”.

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”.

Apple mentioned back in June that the manufacturer was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

'Yellowjackets' Season 3 Recap: What To Remember Before the Horror Thriller's Final Season

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that few demonstrates have been as unhinged as Showtime's Yellowjackets.
  • Industry observers note that when Season 3 kicks off, the Yellowjackets girls' soccer team have actually found a surprising sense of contentment in the wilderness.
  • Ultimately, the group decides that Coach Ben (Steven Krueger) should be killed because of his potential involvement in the destruction of the cabin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that few demonstrates have been as unhinged as Showtime's Yellowjackets. Ever since its premiere in 2021, the series has attracted a large following thanks to its thrilling premise, intriguing storylines set in two different timelines, and endlessly fascinating characters. There are shockingly gruesome scenes (yep, there's cannibalism) and themes like the brutality of girlhood and the long-lasting effects of trauma — but no matter where the story has ventured, it's consistently entertaining to watch. Yellowjackets is returning for its fourth and final season on November 20, so here's a refresher on what went down in Season 3.

Industry observers note that when Season 3 kicks off, the Yellowjackets girls' soccer team have actually found a surprising sense of contentment in the wilderness. They've set up new living conditions after the cabin burned down, and they've officially survived the harsh winter. But the cracks in the society the girls have built start to appear. While Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) has been in charge of the girls as Antler Queen, Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) still believes that she's the group's rightful leader.

Ultimately, the group decides that Coach Ben (Steven Krueger) should be killed because of his potential involvement in the destruction of the cabin. They begin to torture Ben until Natalie puts him out of his misery, adding one more death to the team's tally. This is viewed as a traitorous act, and Natalie is dethroned as Antler Queen, with Shauna stepping in as her replacement. We also learn that the Pit Girl we first witnessed at the very beginning of the series is actually Mari (Alexa Barajas), who unluckily drew the Queen of Hearts card from the deck, and becomes a target for the group to hunt.

The Yellowjackets Season 3 finale features every storyline firing on all cylinders. In the present-day timeline, the mystery of Lottie's (Simone Kessell) death is solved, with the show confirming that Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins) accidentally pushed her down the stairs during an argument. In another twist of fate, Van (Lauren Ambrose) doesn't die from cancer, as fans expected, but is stabbed to death by Melissa (Hilary Swank), who had tried to escape the group's collective past but finds herself drawn back in by her shared connection with her former teammates. Taissa (Tawny Cypress) is devastated by losing Van, and fully descends into madness — cutting out Van's heart, eating it, and burying her love in the wilderness. Shauna also seems to be embracing the unraveling of her life after her family deserts her, while Tai and Misty (Christina Ricci) team up to figure out what to do about Shauna next.

Back in the wilderness, the girls decide on a celebratory feast, intent on gobbling up poor Coach Ben. In the middle of the madness, some researchers stumble across the team, witnessing their cannibalism in the process. Lottie (Courtney Eaton), in the midst of a psychotic episode, murders one of them with an axe. Scientist Hannah (Ashley Sutton) sees an opportunity to survive by teaming up with the girls, and kills her wilderness guide, Kodiak (Joel McHale). Amidst the chaos, the group becomes divided on whether they actually want to be rescued. Van (Liv Hewson) wants to leave the wilderness behind and successfully repairs the scientists' satellite phone, which Natalie climbs to a mountaintop with to send out an SOS that will likely lead to the team's rescue in the final season.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

According to recent reports, your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Industry observers note that your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

According to recent reports, your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

There are still so many questions that Season 4 of Yellowjackets needs to explore. We don't know exactly how the team will be rescued, or how they will be able to fold back into normal society. In the present day, will Shauna successfully win back her family's trust, and what will happen now that Tai and Misty have agreed to team up against her? There has already been so much death for these characters, and it's likely there will be even more bloodshed before the series concludes. Breaking: Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about.
  • The documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing.
  • It has been revealed that now Newly introduced York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about. First-time feature filmmaker Brydie O’Connor’s Sundance-winning documentary “Barbara Forever” is a hypnotic archival collage that retraces the life, work, and death of Barbara Hammer.

The documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing. (Kristen Stewart also jumped on board as an executive producer.) It’s not hard to see why. “Barbara Forever” is an archival documentary that unfolds in the shape and style of its subject, an experimental filmmaker who put together some of the first publicly projected lesbian erotica actually made by a lesbian. Voiceover by the filmmaker spans her early career in the Bay Area (and halcyon days as an out lesbian), her 1992 feature debut “Nitrate Kisses,” and the final years of a cancer battle that ended in 2019. Related Stories Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break.

It has been revealed that now Newly introduced York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met. “I read about Barbara and studied Barbara before I even saw her films,” O’Connor told IndieWire. She reached out to Hammer to “buy her DVDs because they weren’t showing anywhere in D.C. And she wrote back to me. At first, she was a little bit hard on me. She was like, ‘I see you’re writing from an edu.edu address. I just want to make sure that you’re actually a student because if you’re faculty, it would be much, much more expensive.’ [Laughs] And I said, ‘I promise, Barbara, I’m a student. I just can’t wait to see your movies.’ And she sent me her DVDs. So yeah, I think that initial impulse to explore her work was really about … ‘Why don’t more people know about Barbara and her work?'”.

Hammer had degrees in psychology and literature before encountering “Meshes of the Afternoon” director Maya Deren’s films (which also influenced David Lynch) at San Francisco State in the 1970s. They lit the fuse for making her own movies. Circa that time, she’d been living in Santa Rosa and married to a man. She came out as a lesbian — busting through that closet, really, with abandon — and took off with her Super 8 camera to start making lesbian films. Growing up in Kansas, O’Connor, in her early 30s, resonated with Hammer’s early biography, and Hammer’s early lust for self-reinvention.

“She was not really tentative about anything. She picked up a camera in her late 20s as she was getting a divorce from a man when she realized that she was a lesbian and she made her film,” O’Connor said. “She learned by doing. And I was so inspired because, at the time, I was studying American studies and history in school. I had no background in the arts really, except for enjoying consuming them. And I really thought I would be a film critic or a writer… [Barbara Hammer] was not afraid to fail creatively. And she tried so many different ideas, of course, throughout her entire career in making over 85 films, but especially in that first decade of her career.”.

According to recent reports, post-college and in Upcoming York, O’Connor, who’s spent “a decade in the Hammer world, and my entire adult consciousness,” would see Hammer at the Metrograph in Lower Manhattan. “I definitely was ‘the girl who wrote her thesis on Barbara,’ probably one of many, and I was day-playing in the film industry,” O’Connor remarked. “I would occasionally go up to Yale, where her formal archive is held, to continue doing independent research. I was looking at her love letters and her photographs… I wrote to her in January of 2019 when I was about to make my first short film. I said, ‘Hi, Barbara.’ I didn’t know how sick she was at the time. I was like, ‘I’m making my first film. Can I take you to coffee? Do you have any advice for me?’ And she wrote back to me and said, ‘I’m at the very, very end of my life, but best of luck with everything in your career.'”.

It has been revealed that hammer died in March 2019, which is when O’Connor contacted the filmmaker’s partner, the human rights advocate Florrie Burke. “Florrie was the love of her life. They were together for 31 years,” O’Connor said. Their meeting culminated in O’Connor’s 2022 short film “Love, Barbara,” which she expanded into the feature that hit theaters this year. In a 2026 Oscar documentary race heavy on genocide and social challenges — or a three-hour A24 movie that’s shaken up the entire form — “Barbara Forever” is life-affirming, lovely, yet still-vital counter-programming.

Industry observers note that the organic archival rhythm of “Barbara Forever” eschews talking heads altogether, instead conversing with what Hammer’s work looked and felt like. One of the film’s most charming snippets finds Hammer showing one of her (SFW!) films to a classroom of small schoolchildren. They end up having an unexpected appreciation for the experimental film clip’s non-narrative sensibilities.

Recent findings suggest that O’Connor collaborated with Burke on sifting through 35 hours of audio recordings to stitch together a narration unfolding entirely in Hammer’s own words. “Florrie was so happy with [the short], but she always reminded me there’s so much more to Barbara than just our relationship,” O’Connor stated. “Barbara’s this huge personality. She’s so charismatic and charming and really both thoughtful, but also very savvy. She wanted to be recognized. She wanted to be known for her work and her efforts, and she was uncompromising in what she made and how she shared her work. So it just made sense that she would be the narrator of the film.”.

It has been revealed that the Sundance-winning editing, too, proved a challenge, as O’Connor and her filmmaking team pored over more than 400 hours of visual material — from Hammer’s films, to outtakes, B-sides, home videos, and more. “I really wanted to convey with this film: Why did Barbara turn the camera on herself and her life and her lovers and her body as a method of alternative history making? What did she see in the value of that approach and then making experimental cinema out of it and demanding the value of that within culture?”.

Recent findings suggest that that Hammer’s work wasn’t more canonized during her life — an effort O’Connor has made partly her own, especially as a fresh digital restoration of “Nitrate Kisses” is making the rounds — isn’t only because of how confrontational she was about gender and her own sexuality. “Nitrate Kisses” is, after all, an experimental movie about lesbian repression dating back to the early 20th century. Is it also that autofiction and individualism, now a dominant mode of contemporary artistic expression, were also marginalized at that point within her particular corner of the art world?

According to recent reports, “She was both an experimental filmmaker and avant-garde artist and a lesbian filmmaker. And she says, and this was something she remarked all throughout her life and career, that she didn’t fit neatly into either category where she could just build an audience within that space,” O’Connor said. “She really was uncompromising about being both and working at the intersection of both and having both audiences… The experimental film world didn’t necessarily want to see lesbian work, didn’t necessarily want to see the nude woman’s body on screen. And lesbians, there was not so much representation, especially in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, increasingly so, but her work was experimental and thought-provoking, and she felt like a lot of her queer audiences wanted more realistic depictions of queerness.”.

O’Connor, who received a 2026 Creative Capital to not only finish her work on “Barbara Forever” but also continue making docs, said, “The industry is hard, but that certainly won’t stop me from making nonfiction films. I’m just excited to pivot to my next project.”.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's promptly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

In a recent development, this earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her latest direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very rapidly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

Recent findings suggest that she'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time Newly introduced York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The substantial life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

It has been revealed that A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen ….

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Several of the affected companies stated that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme says almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly upgrade all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices.
  • As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too.
  • Industry observers note that as WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an key account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a fresh "View Once" option as well.

Industry observers note that as WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it. WhatsApp also explains that recipients cannot share, forward, save, or take screenshots of View Once text messages. Recipients won't see the text appear in the usual chat interface, either; instead, your recipient will need to open the message in a separate window. Once they close this page, the message disappears.

As mentioned above, this feature is presently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That remarked, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.).

Industry observers note that if you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest patch. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

It is also reminiscent of Netflix's hit spy thriller/dark comedy series Black Doves, which just returned for its 6-part sophomore season earlier this month as well.

In a recent development, the Assassin is far from your standard action thriller due to its complicated mother-son dynamic that is very much the emotional core of the story. Because Edward and Julie are quite opposite in their personalities, their relationship defies typical familial standards in interesting ways. The situation between Julie and Edward only becomes more nuanced in The Assassin season 2, as new secrets are revealed that have the potential to ruin the efforts they made in season 1 to make amends.

Edward attempts to convince Julie to change her ways, disapproving of her life choices, while Julie is reluctant to change and doesn't take Edward's criticisms. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tendo Nagenda, a former executive on Netflix’s film team, has been tapped as president of Proximity Media, the production company founded by Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler, and Sev Ohanian, the founders declared Thursday.

Nagenda spent four years at Netflix under film chief Scott Stuber, exiting in 2022, and in that time he shepherded films like Spike Lee’s “Da 5 Bloods,” “The Old Guard,” “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom,” “The Harder They Fall,” and “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery.”.

Industry observers note that nagenda will oversee all aspects of creative development and production at Proximity, including its film, TV, and non-fiction divisions, and will report directly to the founders. The heads of Film, Television and Nonfiction will all report directly to Nagenda, and he’ll work alongside marketing and operations lead Terra Potts and music lead Ludwig Göransson. He starts on November 30. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition.

In a recent development, “Tendo has spent his career working alongside talented filmmakers, championing original ideas, and helping make projects that resonate with audiences around the world,” mentioned Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler and Ohanian in a joint statement. “As Proximity continues to grow across film, television, and nonfiction, we’re excited to have his creative instincts and experience helping guide this next chapter. He shares our belief in the power of storytelling to connect people, challenge perspectives and create meaningful impact, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the team.”.

“I’m honored and excited to join Ryan, Zinzi, Sev, and the entire Proximity team,” remarked Nagenda. “Their commitment to ambitious, meaningful storytelling reflects everything I’ve always believed in, and I look forward to building on what they’ve created, collaborating with extraordinary filmmakers and creators, and bringing compelling latest stories to audiences around the world.”.

Industry observers note that since leaving Netflix in 2022, Nagenda launched 10 by Ten Entertainment, which produced and released Jeymes Samuel’s “The Book of Clarence” in 2024. Prior to working at Netflix, he had a long track record at Disney and oversaw films on the live-action slate, including “Beauty and the Beast,” “Cinderella,” “Saving Mr. Banks,” “Mulan,” “A Wrinkle in Time,” and “Queen of Katwe.”.

Proximity Media had a banner year last year with the release of “Sinners,” which grossed $365 million worldwide. Some of its other features have included “Judas and the Black Messiah,” “Space Jam: A Latest Legacy,” and “Creed III.” It’s now working on a reboot of “The X-Files” for Hulu starring Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel. Proximity recently entered into a multiyear TV deal with Netflix for scripted and unscripted projects. And it also has produced some nonfiction work including Nat Geo’s hit “Hurricane Katrina: Race Against Time,” as well as other titles like “Stephen Curry: Underrated,” “Homeroom,” and “Anthem.”.

It has been revealed that nagenda is a graduate of Claremont McKenna College and a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and Producers United. He also serves on the Social Services Committee of the Motion Picture & Television Fund and the board of the UCLA Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

Tech Report: I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better?
  • You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up.
  • Recent findings suggest that proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—presently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Recent findings suggest that proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—presently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

According to recent reports, as the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

Recent findings suggest that for the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it.".

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

According to recent reports, however, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

In a recent development, next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Recent findings suggest that here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

It has been revealed that I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran highlighted that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

It has been revealed that increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first six episodes of 9-1-1: Nashville's second season have seen the first responders and other characters deal with a mysterious killer called the Pharoah (A.J. Buckley), who's been terrorizing Nashville with murders inspired by the Biblical plagues. The mid-season finale is an explosive episode that sees the Pharoah escalate things with his latest scheme after he catches Rogue (Ryan Phillippe) trying to lure him into a trap. As of the end of the mid-season finale, the first responders were able to save the group of children that the Pharoah just targeted, but Don (Chris O'Donnell) and Rogue are right now caught in his latest trap.

Sources indicate that following the mid-season finale for Season 2, 9-1-1: Nashville's showrunner, Rashad Raisani, sat down with Collider to talk about the episode and break down the first half of the season. Raisani discusses that shocking cliffhanger, 9-1-1: Nashville's expansion into the crime thriller genre this season, and the compelling character dynamics that have been at the center of this season. He also teases some storylines from the back half of Season 2, including the upcoming crossover with 9-1-1.

So, the Pharaoh has finally been revealed in this great moment where Don has stopped to help this stranger, right after viewers have found out what the Pharaoh looks like. We see Don weigh this decision for a moment, because he has ice and a cake in his car, and he's already cutting it close to the baby shower. Why do you think he ultimately chose to stop?

According to recent reports, RASHAD RAISANI: I think Don stopped because that's who he is: if he sees somebody stranded on the side of the road with a smoking car, he's always going to help. And Pharaoh knows that 100%. That would be Don's greatest weakness: there's no way he's going to pass by somebody who needs help and not help them.

That cliffhanger was already very intense with the Pharaoh taking Don, only for it to then be revealed that he has Rogue as well. How early on in the season did you know you wanted to end the mid-season finale with both of them in danger, and why is it specifically these two characters?

Industry observers note that RAISANI: I think we knew pretty early that we wanted there to be a massive price that they had to pay. Pharoah warns them in the second episode, “Don't interfere, or else there will be consequences,” so I think we knew early that we were going to do something big with them. And I think it always had to be Don and Rogue because – along with Cammie (Kimberly Williams-Paisley), who's the dispatcher, who does the most to try and stop Pharaoh — Don's fire team has saved many of his victims, and Rogue is in charge of trying to catch this guy. So, it made a lot of sense for him to take two of the three most vital people who were both firstborns as his way of exacting revenge and proving his point that there would be consequences.

Sources indicate that there was an interesting clash this episode between Rogue and Nick, when they fight over Rogue’s unconventional approach vs. Nick’s by-the-book FBI approach, and Nick makes a comment about Rogue's past of rule-breaking in New York. We already know about Rogue’s wife's death and the Strangler case, but there's also been some mystery about why he moved to Nashville in the first place. How much can you tease about Rogue's past in New York and this reputation of his that Nick’s referring to?

Recent findings suggest that RAISANI: Well, I think I can say it was a reputation well-earned, that Rogue did break some things, and that he bent the rules for some people, maybe a little too much. And so I think that will be definitely something that comes out and continues to get revisited, and we'll see that tendency of Rogue’s come out even more and lead to some problems in Nashville as well. So it's definitely in his character. Nick is right onto it when he states that, and it will lead to more clashes, frankly, between them. So, yeah, it's going to be a part of things.

It has been revealed that alongside the Pharaoh, there's this really compelling villain this season in Marcia Zellner (Camryn Manheim), who continues to make the disturbing prank calls to Cammie this episode while showing no remorse and still being her friend at work. How did you decide to have this additional villain in Zellner, who's completely separate from the Pharaoh, and is there anything you can hint about her motivation in targeting Cammie specifically?

RAISANI: Marcia is a direct inspiration from Ryan Murphy. It was one of the substantial things he wanted to do this season: he wanted to have a mysterious criminal; he wanted to have Cammie be tormented by somebody like Camryn Manheim, who ended up being Camryn Manheim, who, at a certain pivotal moment, would be prank-calling Cammie, and then take off a wig and reveal scars, and you [realize], “Oh my god, she has a big problem.” So, we knew early we wanted to do that, and we wanted to explore these two things, and we wanted these two balls in the air about Pharaoh and Marcia, and we're not necessarily saying that they aren't related.

Like, we want the audience to just wonder. It's possible, on the one hand, that bad things can be happening at the same time that they're unrelated; it's also possible that they're connected. It's also possible that Marcia might be using the stress of Pharaoh too, for her own motivation, to torment Cammie even more. So, I think that was part of what made us feel like it'd be fun to have another crazy thing from left field, to suddenly have multiple fronts of badness. And then Marcia is coming from a very specific place, a very specific incident that corroded her, and that led her to become the person she is now, and that has made her so determined to torment and torture Cammie.

It has been revealed that ryan (Michael Provost) showed a particular interest in the Pharaoh investigation, and we saw him do some detective work with Rogue this season. Was it just about this particular case for him, or does he have more of a real interest in this, and could he be more involved in this alongside Rogue once he goes back to work?

RAISANI: I think yes. I think, first, he was just taken by this guy who, Ryan – Michael Provost’s character – is very rule-following; he’s grown up as a rule follower, he was always trying to please Dad, and he's done a good job of that, but then he watches this guy from Newly introduced York come in and just break all the rules and be a maverick, and there's something very alluring to Ryan, because he's so different than anything Ryan's ever seen, and so Ryan is really enchanted by him.

And I think it really starts from a character level that he was so fascinated by Rogue, and then he starts to get into the investigation, because he's so excited to be around Rogue. So I think that there is a definite chance that he'll continue to pursue law enforcement, and to continue working with Rogue. But Ryan has his own drama to get through; his wife has cancer, she's pregnant, he’s going to take time off from the firehouse… He's got to juggle that also with the things that he's interested in doing at work.

So, Ryan's going to be taking a whole month off work for Sam (MacKenzie Porter); how much of their journey are we going to see in the back half of the season while Ryan's away from the 113?

Sources indicate that RAISANI: There's going to be some episodes where they’ll be offscreen for a bit, because they have to go and travel, as he stated, but then we are going to do a really rich story devoted to what her surgery looks like, what the post-surgery looks like, what the caretaking looks like, and explore what that journey is for them, and how it also affects our other characters. So, it's going to be a huge part. And then, tracking her pregnancy and her cancer through the back half of the season is going to be a major driver for us.

Will another firefighter be brought in temporarily to replace Ryan at the 113?

RAISANI: No. But we will play, we will dramatize how the leadership void... him being gone, their Lieutenant's gone — that does change the pecking order a little bit, and it will force our other characters to see who's going to step up and fill that, and that's kind of where we play in those episodes.

Don and Blythe (Jessica Capshaw) had a major breakthrough last episode, and they seem to be on solid ground this episode. Blythe and Dixie (LeAnne Rimes) are still clearly in conflict with each other, but are Don and Blythe completely past the hurdle of Dixie in their marriage?

RAISANI: I don't know about completely… I mean, I think the wound is always there, but they're healing; that's what I would say. They are healing from it. And I think it's always going to be a memory. It's like, they say you can forgive without forgetting, and I think they're now in that stage, that they are getting back to solid ground.

Industry observers note that it doesn't mean Dixie's going to disappear, and it doesn't mean Blythe and Dixie don't have their own relationship and their own frenemy status, because they are now hitched together with this record label that Blythe's in charge of, and we're going to play some stories in that world, where we're going to find out that those two women, as much as they can't stand each other all the time, they actually work really well together, and they complement each other. We're going to play the fun and the irony of them being kind of stuck together and thriving together.

What lessons did you learn while showrunning Lone Star that you've taken with you to Nashville?

In a recent development, RAISANI: That’s a great question. What I've learned, and it's still the hard way, is that you never have enough time to do all the things you want. And that you just end up... like, on Lone Star, our last season went from 18 episodes to 16 episodes to 12 episodes, and suddenly, the character arcs got smushed, and smushed, and smushed, so that Marjan (Natacha Karam) would have to meet the parents in the same episode that they introduced her fiancé, [and it's] the same episode where she has to get married, whereas that would normally take three or four episodes. So what I've learned is that you always need to have good drive for the characters, but you don't have to have them do a bunch of different things in tight clumps; the audience will go with them on their journeys.

And then the other thing I've learned is how to do these big action cases and how to interweave them, and that if you don't.... if the case is – and we've been guilty of it before, where we just did a big case for a big case, but the best cases have an emotional connection to what's happening in the characters' lives, and that makes them much richer. And I think that was the biggest lesson of Lone Star, we were at our best when those things were in sync with each other.

According to recent reports, rogue has been such a great addition to the season. The Pharaoh investigation has tied his storylines to that of the 113 thus far in every episode, but have there been challenges in navigating the process of weaving him into personal storylines as well and determining how he'll stay connected to them after this case?

RAISANI: I think so. I mean, I think that the good news is that because Ryan was so wrapped up in the case at the beginning, and because Don, as the season goes along, gets more inevitably put in the center of this, it hasn't been that hard to keep Rogue with our characters. I think the hardest challenge now is that if we're telling a call center story, and we're telling a story about Pharaoh, it just sometimes can be harder to play some of our — what I also love to do — firehouse family scenes. That's been our biggest juggling act, we're still turning the dials on how to balance everything with telling this hard-driven thriller mystery.

Cammie has this crazy boss, Marcia, who's tormenting her in a psychological thriller, but we also don't want to give short shrift to our beloved characters in the firehouse. And I think, to be honest, that's been one of the biggest things I've been wanting us to kind of figure out how to do better, frankly, in the back half of the season: just bringing some of that joy that comes from people like Taylor (Hailey Kilgore), and Blue (Hunter McVey), and Roxie (Juani Feliz), and the firehouse, because I think that's where a lot of the warmth of our show comes from. And so how do you balance them? How do you get Dixie in the show when there's this mysterious killer killing people?

Sources indicate that the mid-season finale had me on the edge of my seat the entire time, and Season 2 in general has had really heightened stakes, both on the calls and outside of them, through the introduction of the Pharaoh. What's the process been like of expanding the genre of 9-1-1: Nashville this season beyond both the procedural model and the family drama aspect to include the crime thriller element?

According to recent reports, RAISANI: Now, I’ve absolutely loved it. I mean, I've just been thrilled. I've always loved police thrillers. Whether it be, you know, True Detective, or Sherlock, or Seven, or Zodiac. And so I think to infuse that, I think it ended up being… I never knew how it was going to work, but I think that blend of taking our heightened Nashville fun and soap, and then giving it this bass note of a real high-stakes killer and thriller, and somebody like Rogue, who's very hard-bitten. I think it ended up, to me, making the chemistry all work better. And so, it's been a joy. I love crime thrillers, and I think that's one thing that's evident. Our writers love it, the actors love it, and so I think it's really elevated the show to have that.

And this episode revealed another piece of backstory for Rogue. We already knew about his sons, but he also has a little sister who's seven years younger. Is this a potential character that we could see in the future?

RAISANI: It is, as are his sons. And we will see one of his sons very soon. So yes, every time we make those little stray comments, we're trying to tell – and our audience is so smart, they're just like you, up on it. They always go, “Oh, I see what you're doing.” But yeah, we want to world-build, and we want to let people know that these people have lives off the few minutes of screen time they get in an episode, that they do have rich backstories and lives, and we will be bringing them in.

Can I ask, is his son going to be in the LA crossover with 9-1-1?

And then, Don and Rogue have come a long way from Don briefly letting him choke in the season premiere to them now having a friendship. What do you think the shift was for Don to finally trust him?

RAISANI: I think the shift was that Don began to respect that Rogue has integrity. He may not be everybody's cup of tea; he may be gruff, he may be a little bit more brusque than anything Don's used to, but Don sees what guides him is goodness, even if it has an interesting package, and they don't agree on how to do things, and they don't agree on how to talk to people even sometimes. At the end of the day, Don sees that Rogue is a force for good, in his own, sometimes misguided, way – at least, misguided in Don's opinion. And so I think he sees the light in Rogue, even if Rogue isn't the guy he would have imagined he'd want to hang out with.

There are so many great dynamics amongst the main characters in Nashville, especially now that Rogue is also in the picture. Are there any dynamics we haven't seen yet between characters who haven't had much cause to interact, that you would love to play around with?

RAISANI: Yeah. I mean, there's a lot. One thing that we just scratched the surface of, funny enough, is Taylor with Don. I think Taylor and Roxie is one of the great friendships we just haven't had the time for yet, but that's coming in the back half of the season, is to play more of Taylor and Roxie's friendship, to play more of Rogue with people like Cammie, who I think — and Blythe — he has great chemistry with them.

Recent findings suggest that I feel like we're just getting started. There's so many people who’ve never really had scenes, or certainly not stories, together. So I'd like to see Dixie meet Rogue. They have a brush in an episode that's coming up, so I like to think we're just getting started. There are so many relationships we haven't even… we haven't even seen Blythe’s dad, Edward (Tim Matheson), so far this season. So, like I noted, I always feel like we're running out of time before we even get started.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, director Brian Duffield is a cinephile who watches a lot of movies, but when the time came to direct his adventure film “Whalefall” he was dismayed to realize he couldn’t think of a single film he could look to as a model. “It was a nightmare for that reason,” Duffield told IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “It also the joy of it, having a room full of amazingly gifted artists all starting from this place of real befuddlement.”.

In the movie, Austin Abrams plays a scuba diver who gets swallowed by a sperm whale and has only an hour of oxygen to keep him alive while he tries to escape; it’s a premise that posed multiple challenges for Duffield and his team, starting with the question of how exactly to build the stomach that Abrams would be trapped inside for the majority of the film — and how to shoot those scenes. Related Stories Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel.

Industry observers note that “It wasn’t normal coverage,” Duffield said. “Even a shot of Austin just sitting in the stomach required months of preparation and planning — every shot of him in the stomach is, by its nature, a stunt.” The ultimate effect onscreen is terrifying, but on set Duffield says the stomach scenes looked more than a little ridiculous. “The set looked crazy. From the outside it’s this black weird bag, and then it’s on a gimbal so it’s moving, and it’s full of water.”.

Recent findings suggest that to give the impression of the stomach chewing, Duffield’s crew found an old-school, practical solution. “When the stomach chews, it compresses,” Duffield said. “The way we did that is we just had burly men jump onto it. Austin’s inside, and there’s a guy with a camera, and I can’t fit in the stomach so I’m just watching these New Zealanders leap and compress, then I’m hearing Austin scream.” Although Duffield planned his shots meticulously, he often found that the stomach had a mind of its own and required swift adaptation from the crew.

It has been revealed that “There’s water in the stomach, and we would drain it every night,” Duffield stated. “The material that the stomach was made of would change shape overnight, and we’d come back to resume a scene, and our set would be a different set — we’d fill it with water, and it would all lay different.” Doors also contracted due to humidity and other conditions. “By the end of the shoot, there were so many jagged doors that we’d cut for cameras.”.

Industry observers note that ultimately, all of Duffield’s storyboards “went out the window” because the stomach kept changing shape, and Abrams couldn’t roll in the planned directions. “The stomach was kind of directing the movie,” Duffield said. “Austin and I had to sync up and figure out how, with this newly introduced environment every day, to get the shots that tell the story as cleanly as possible.” That was no easy task, especially since the set’s very nature made it hard to acclimate the audience geographically.

“It sounds ridiculous, but we had so many conversations about trying to get an audience to see that ‘that sphincter leads to the throat,’ or ‘that sphincter leads to the second stomach,'” Duffield mentioned, adding that he constantly had to think about how one shot would connect to another to let the audience know where Abrams was inside the whale. “Austin’s moving around the whole time, and the stomach goes in every direction. Bit by bit, shot by shot, every shot is its own unique challenge.”.

Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron worked with Duffield and the camera team to come up with visual cues that could help the audience follow Abrams’ journey through the whale, but the task was further complicated by the fact that the audience was sharing his point of view — and for long portions of the story, Abrams’ character was supposed to be confused. “Austin’s character doesn’t have a lot of information about what is happening to him,” Duffield remarked. “You want the audience to have the same information as him, but not get so lost and confused that they’re out of the movie.”.

Recent findings suggest that duffield knew that striking that balance would be tricky throughout production and editing. “It’s hard to have a character in a situation he doesn’t know anything about and then have an audience get invested,” Duffield stated, adding that the usual test screening questions were useless here. “It’s the classic test screening thing: ‘Is there anything that’s confusing to you?'” Luckily, Duffield worked with master editor Pietro Scalia, who worked with the director to find the most straightforward way to connect the audience to the material.

“We eventually concluded, just focus on Austin,” Duffield mentioned. “Austin is dynamite, and he’s carrying you, and the more you’re in lockstep with Austin, you’re going to be okay.” The key, Duffield felt, was to preserve the illusion of reality at every possible moment. “ When we were editing and sound designing, it was just like, ‘How do we keep trying to make it feel real?’ I’m a very pro-CG guy, but even if there’s some stitching from a stuntman or a digital double to Austin, Austin’s in every shot of the scene. I think some of the things that people think is a digital double are not a digital double — it’s Austin just getting yanked around and fighting for his life.”.

In a recent development, though Duffield is sure Abrams wouldn’t want to return for a sequel, he mentioned his lead actor was as up for the physical demands of the role as the department heads were for the mental and logistical challenges — challenges unlike any they had ever faced. “Nothing any of us had done before applied to this project,” Duffield said, adding that nothing they learned would apply to future projects given the singular nature of “Whalefall.” “It was really challenging, but I was looking for that kind of filmmaking challenge. It was the hardest shoot I’ll probably ever have, but everyone was also giddy about it.”.
